questions.stem: An 82-year-old client in a long-term care facility has a pressure injury on the left heel covered by dry, black eschar. The eschar is firmly attached and intact, with no surrounding redness, swelling, bogginess, or drainage. A newly hired nurse suggests applying a moist dressing to soften the eschar so it can be removed. Which action by the charge nurse is most appropriate?
options: Apply the moist dressing so the eschar softens and lifts away
Keep the eschar intact, offload the heel, and inspect it every shift
Score the eschar with a scalpel so a prescribed debriding agent can penetrate it
Start wet-to-dry dressings to pull the black tissue off the heel
optionRationales: Incorrect. Softening stable heel eschar removes its protective cover and opens a route for infection; it is left in place unless the provider orders otherwise.

Correct. Dry, firmly attached heel eschar with no redness, bogginess, or drainage is stable and acts as the body's natural cover, so it is usually left in place while the heel is offloaded and monitored.
Incorrect. Cutting into eschar is sharp debridement, which is performed by a surgeon, and stable heel eschar is not targeted for removal.
Incorrect. Wet-to-dry is nonselective and painful, and stable heel eschar is not debrided without a specific provider order.
questions.rationale: The RYB guide says black eschar is debrided, but stable heel eschar is the key exception. When heel eschar is dry, firmly attached, and intact with no redness, swelling, bogginess, or drainage, it works as a natural protective cover and is usually left in place. The nurse offloads the heel to remove pressure and inspects the eschar every shift for signs that it is becoming unstable. The tempting choice is the moist dressing because “black = debride,” but softening stable heel eschar strips away its protection without a provider order.
questions.takeaway: Stable heel eschar (dry, intact, firmly attached, no redness or drainage) is left in place and the heel is offloaded.
questions.hintContent: Think about the one location where black eschar is treated differently, and what makes eschar “stable.”
questions.hintStrategy: When a rule has a well-known exception, check whether the stem's details (location, dryness, no drainage) trigger the exception before applying the general rule.

questions.stem: A client with a Stage 4 sacral pressure injury that is 70% yellow slough has a prescription for wet-to-dry saline gauze dressings every 8 hours. During the last dressing removal, the client cried out and rated pain 8 on a 0–10 scale. The next change is due in 45 minutes, and an oral analgesic is prescribed as needed. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Ask the provider about switching to a less painful debridement method
Soak the dried gauze with saline so it lifts off without pulling
Give the prescribed analgesic just before removing the old gauze
Give the prescribed analgesic now so it peaks during the dressing change
optionRationales: Incorrect. Discussing a gentler method is reasonable later, but the next change is due in 45 minutes and the client needs pain control for this one now.
Incorrect. The drying gauze is what pulls the slough off; soaking it first defeats the mechanical debridement the provider prescribed.
Incorrect. Premedicating is right, but an oral analgesic given just before the change will not peak until after the gauze is already off.
Correct. Wet-to-dry removal is predictably painful, so premedicating 30–60 minutes ahead lets the analgesic reach its peak effect when the gauze is removed.
questions.rationale: Mechanical debridement with wet-to-dry gauze works because the gauze dries onto the wound and pulls nonviable tissue away when it is removed. That same action is nonselective and painful, so the nurse anticipates pain and premedicates before the procedure rather than reacting during it. Giving the oral analgesic now times its peak effect for the dressing change in 45 minutes. Soaking the gauze is tempting because it reduces pain, but it stops the gauze from pulling off the slough and defeats the purpose of the prescription.
questions.takeaway: Expect wet-to-dry removal to hurt: premedicate before the change instead of soaking the gauze.
questions.hintContent: Recall why wet-to-dry gauze is allowed to dry before it is removed, and what that means for the client's comfort.
questions.hintStrategy: For a procedure known to be painful, look for the option that prevents the pain before it starts without undoing the treatment itself.

questions.stem: Last week, a client's Stage 3 hip pressure injury was documented as 100% red granulation with scant serous drainage. Today, after cleansing, the nurse finds soft yellow slough covering 30% of the wound bed and a new 1-cm patch of black tissue at one edge. The client is afebrile. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Measure and document the changes, report them, and request a revised plan
Continue the current plan, because new slough is a normal part of wound healing
Document the changes and recheck the wound at the next dressing change
Turn the client more often and reassess the wound in 2 days
optionRationales: Correct. New yellow and black tissue in a once-clean wound signals deterioration; the nurse documents objectively, reports, and asks for the plan to be reassessed and revised.
Incorrect. New slough and eschar in a previously clean red wound mean the wound is deteriorating, not progressing.
Incorrect. Documenting is needed, but a deteriorating wound must also be reported so the plan can be revised; waiting delays care.
Incorrect. More pressure relief is helpful, but it is only part of the plan; the deterioration still needs to be reported and the full plan revised.
questions.rationale: The RYB guide is also a way to track a wound over time: black and yellow should shrink and red should grow. When a wound that was 100% red granulation develops new slough and eschar, it is deteriorating, which is a red flag. The nurse measures and documents the change, reports it, and asks for the plan of care (pressure relief, moisture, nutrition, debridement) to be revised. Continuing the current plan is the tempting distractor, but slough is never an expected step after clean granulation.
questions.takeaway: New slough or eschar in a previously clean red wound means deterioration: document, report, and revise the plan.
questions.hintContent: Compare this week's colors with last week's. Which direction should a healing wound move on the RYB guide?
questions.hintStrategy: In evaluate-outcome items, compare current data with the baseline; a change in the wrong direction calls for reporting and a revised plan.

questions.stem: The nurse is changing the dressing on a client's Stage 4 sacral pressure injury and must estimate the percentage of red, yellow, and black tissue for the weekly wound note. The old dressing has been removed, and the nurse has performed hand hygiene and put on clean gloves. Which action should the nurse take next?
options: Record the color percentages before the wound is disturbed
Apply the prescribed enzymatic ointment to the black areas
Cleanse the wound with the prescribed solution, then assess it
Pack the wound loosely to absorb drainage during the assessment
optionRationales: Incorrect. Old drainage and debris can look like slough, so estimating before cleansing gives an inaccurate assessment.
Incorrect. Treatment comes after the wound is cleansed and assessed, so the nurse knows exactly where the eschar is.
Correct. The wound is cleansed first so that old drainage and loose debris are not mistaken for slough, and then the colors are estimated.
Incorrect. Packing hides the wound bed and is not part of assessment; it would make color estimation impossible.
questions.rationale: Accurate wound assessment depends on seeing the actual wound bed. Old exudate and loose debris left on the surface can look like yellow slough and distort the percentages. The first step in the nurse's wound-care sequence is to cleanse, then assess size, stage, and the percentage of red, yellow, and black tissue, and only then apply the prescribed treatment. Recording percentages immediately is tempting because it seems like “assess first,” but an assessment of an uncleansed wound is not accurate.
questions.takeaway: Cleanse the wound before estimating red, yellow, and black percentages.
questions.hintContent: Think about what on the wound surface could be mistaken for slough if the wound is not cleaned first.
questions.hintStrategy: “Assess before act” still requires a valid assessment; pick the step that makes the assessment accurate.

questions.stem: During a night shift, a client's sacral pressure injury has a loose, lifting edge of black eschar. The charge nurse tells a newly licensed nurse, “The surgeon is busy. Just trim the loose black edge with the sterile scissors.” Which response by the newly licensed nurse is most appropriate?
options: “I'll trim only the black part and stop before I reach any red tissue.”
“That's sharp debridement, which the surgeon does. I'll notify the surgeon.”
“I won't cut it, but I'll document the loose black edge in the chart.”
“I'll trim it only if the surgeon gives me a phone order to do it.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Limiting the cut does not make it within the nurse's role; cutting away eschar is still sharp debridement.
Correct. Sharp debridement is performed by the surgeon; the nurse reports the finding and follows the prescribed plan.
Incorrect. Declining is correct and documenting is needed, but the changed eschar must also be reported to the surgeon so it can be managed.
Incorrect. Getting the surgeon involved is right, but an order does not expand the nurse's scope; sharp debridement is still performed by the surgeon.
questions.rationale: Nurses can debride with limitations. Mechanical (wet-to-dry), chemical (enzymatic), and autolytic methods are nursing actions carried out with a prescription, but cutting dead tissue away with a scalpel or scissors is sharp debridement, which is performed by the surgeon. A charge nurse's instruction does not expand the newly licensed nurse's scope, so the safe response is to decline and report the finding to the surgeon. Trimming “only the black part” is tempting because it sounds careful, but it is still a sharp debridement procedure outside the nurse's role.
questions.takeaway: Cutting away eschar is sharp debridement by the surgeon, even if another nurse says to do it.
questions.hintContent: Decide which debridement method the instruction describes and who performs that method.
questions.hintStrategy: When an instruction from a colleague conflicts with scope of practice, choose the response that declines the task and uses the proper channel.

questions.stem: For 10 days, a client's Stage 3 trochanter pressure injury has been treated with prescribed wet-to-dry dressings to remove yellow slough. Today, after cleansing, the wound bed is 100% beefy red, moist, and bumpy, with a thin pink rim at the edges. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Continue the wet-to-dry dressings because they are clearly working
Stop the wet-to-dry gauze and apply a moist protective dressing
Document the healthy granulation and reassess at the next change
Contact the provider to change to a dressing that protects the red tissue
optionRationales: Incorrect. The debridement goal has been met; continuing nonselective wet-to-dry would now tear away the healthy granulation tissue.
Incorrect. A moist protective dressing is the right goal, but the nurse cannot change a prescribed treatment without a new order from the provider.
Incorrect. Documenting the improvement is appropriate, but the wet-to-dry order would keep stripping new tissue until the provider changes it.
Correct. The wound is now all granulation, so the RYB goal has shifted to protect and keep moist; the nonselective wet-to-dry order needs to be changed.
questions.rationale: The RYB goal follows the wound as it changes. Wet-to-dry dressings were appropriate while the wound held yellow slough, but now the bed is 100% beefy red granulation with new epithelium at the edges, so the goal has shifted to protect. Because wet-to-dry gauze is nonselective, it would now strip away the healthy tissue the client has just grown. Continuing the current order is tempting because the treatment “worked,” but the nurse must recognize that the goal has been met and contact the provider to change the plan.
questions.takeaway: When a debrided wound becomes all red granulation, the goal becomes protect, so a wet-to-dry order needs to be changed.
questions.hintContent: Re-apply the RYB guide to today's wound bed, not to the wound as it looked 10 days ago.
questions.hintStrategy: In evaluation items, ask whether the original goal has been met; if it has, the right action is usually to change the plan.

questions.stem: The nurse receives a hand-off report on four clients with pressure injuries. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client with a necrotic sacral wound, foul purulent drainage, fever of 38.9 °C, and new confusion
A client with dry, intact, firmly attached heel eschar and no redness around it
A client whose red, granulating sacral wound bled slightly when the last dressing was removed this morning
A client with a 60% yellow sacral wound whose wet-to-dry change is due in 2 hours
optionRationales: Correct. Purulent drainage, fever, and a change in mental status suggest a spreading wound infection that could progress to sepsis; this client is unstable.
Incorrect. This describes stable heel eschar, which is left in place and monitored; it is not urgent.
Incorrect. Healthy granulation is fragile and bleeds easily; slight bleeding is an expected finding.
Incorrect. A scheduled dressing change for a stable wound can wait until the unstable client is assessed.
questions.rationale: Prioritize the client whose data suggest a systemic, worsening problem. Necrotic tissue feeds bacteria, and new foul purulent drainage with high fever and new confusion signals a serious wound infection with possible systemic spread. That client needs immediate assessment and a prompt report to the provider. Slight bleeding from granulation is tempting because bleeding sounds urgent, but fragile granulation tissue is expected to bleed a little when touched.
questions.takeaway: Fever, purulent drainage, and new confusion in a client with a necrotic wound take priority over expected or routine wound findings.
questions.hintContent: Separate the expected wound findings from the one that suggests infection affecting the whole body.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for systemic changes (fever, mental status) layered on a local finding; acute and unstable beats expected and routine.

questions.stem: A client is receiving a prescribed enzymatic debriding ointment for a Stage 4 sacral pressure injury. On rounds, the nurse finds the client lying supine, and the turning record shows no position change for the last 3 hours. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Check the sacral wound for new damage before moving the client
Report the missed turns to the charge nurse for follow-up
Turn the client off the sacrum and resume a scheduled turning plan
Ask the provider whether sharp debridement would speed up healing
optionRationales: Incorrect. Assessing the wound is important, but the client is still lying on the sacrum; relieving pressure comes first, and the wound can be checked once turned.
Incorrect. Reporting the lapse is reasonable, but it does not relieve the pressure that is damaging the sacrum right now.
Correct. Debridement treats the wound, not its cause; relieving pressure on the sacrum right away protects the wound and the tissue around it.
Incorrect. The immediate problem is ongoing pressure on the wound; changing the debridement method would not remove it.
questions.rationale: Debridement removes dead tissue, but it does not treat the cause of a pressure injury. As long as the client lies on the sacrum, pressure keeps squeezing off blood flow and the wound cannot heal, no matter how well the eschar is debrided. The first action is to relieve the pressure by turning the client off the sacrum and restarting a reliable turning plan. Asking about faster debridement is tempting, but it focuses on the wound treatment while the cause of the injury is still happening.
questions.takeaway: Debridement treats the wound, not the cause; pressure relief must continue.
questions.hintContent: Ask what is causing harm to this client right now, and whether the ointment addresses that cause.
questions.hintStrategy: When a stem shows an ongoing hazard, choose the action that stops the hazard before actions that fine-tune treatment.

questions.stem: A client with a sacral pressure injury containing yellow slough is receiving prescribed wet-to-dry dressings. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider?
options: Pain rated 6 on a 0–10 scale while the dried gauze is being removed
Spreading redness and warmth around the wound with a temperature of 38.4 °C
Pinpoint bleeding from red areas of the wound bed right after the gauze is removed
Strands of yellow tissue stuck to the dried gauze after it is removed
optionRationales: Incorrect. Wet-to-dry removal is expected to be painful; the nurse manages it with premedication rather than reporting it as a new problem.
Correct. Spreading redness, warmth, and fever are signs of wound infection, which is more likely in wounds containing dead tissue and must be reported.
Incorrect. Small bleeding points from fragile granulation are expected with nonselective wet-to-dry removal.
Incorrect. Slough on the removed gauze shows the mechanical debridement is working as intended.
questions.rationale: Wounds that contain dead tissue are at higher risk for infection, so the nurse watches for increasing pain, spreading redness and warmth, purulent or foul drainage, fever, and a rising WBC. Spreading redness with warmth and fever is a new, abnormal finding that needs to be reported. The other findings are expected effects of wet-to-dry debridement: it is painful, it can cause small bleeding points, and it pulls slough onto the gauze. Pinpoint bleeding is the tempting choice, but it comes from fragile granulation and is not a sign of a complication by itself.
questions.takeaway: Spreading redness, warmth, and fever in a wound with dead tissue suggest infection; report them.
questions.hintContent: Sort the findings into expected effects of wet-to-dry debridement versus signs of a new complication.
questions.hintStrategy: For “which finding should be reported,” eliminate everything the treatment is expected to cause, then pick the new abnormal finding.

questions.stem: A client has three pressure injuries: a sacral wound that is 80% black eschar, a right heel wound covered by dry, intact, firmly attached eschar with no redness or drainage, and a trochanter wound that is 100% red granulation. While planning care, the nurse reviews which wound needs prescribed debridement. Which wound should the nurse identify?
options: The sacral and heel wounds, because both contain black eschar
The heel wound, because all black eschar must be debrided
The trochanter wound, because red tissue must be kept clean and moist
The sacral wound, because its eschar must be removed for healing
optionRationales: Incorrect. The sacral wound does need debridement, but stable heel eschar that is dry, intact, and firmly attached is left in place as a natural cover.
Incorrect. Stable heel eschar that is dry, intact, and firmly attached is usually left in place as a natural cover.
Incorrect. Red granulation is kept clean and moist, but that is protection, not debridement; there is no dead tissue to remove.
Correct. Black eschar in the sacral wound blocks healing and feeds bacteria, so it needs debridement; it is not covered by the heel exception.
questions.rationale: Apply the RYB guide wound by wound. Black eschar must be debrided for healing, so the sacral wound with 80% eschar needs debridement. The heel eschar is black too, but it is dry, intact, firmly attached, and free of redness and drainage, so it is stable and usually left in place as a natural cover. The heel is the tempting answer because it is black, while the trochanter wound is all red granulation that should be protected, not debrided.
questions.takeaway: Debride black eschar except stable heel eschar; protect red granulation.
questions.hintContent: Apply the RYB goal to each wound separately, and remember the one location where black is handled differently.
questions.hintStrategy: When several items share a feature (black tissue), look for the stem detail that makes one of them an exception.

questions.stem: During a dressing change on a client's Stage 3 pressure injury, a nursing student says the yellow tissue in the wound must be slough. The nurse notes that the yellow tissue is lumpy, firm, and part of the wound wall, and it does not wipe away during gentle cleansing. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
options: It is likely living subcutaneous fat, which should be protected, not removed
It is slough, which should be cleansed away at every dressing change from now on
It is early eschar that will turn black and require debridement
It is purulent exudate that confirms a wound infection
optionRationales: Correct. Lumpy yellow tissue that is part of the wound wall is subcutaneous fat, which is living tissue and a Stage 3 clue; it is not a debridement target.
Incorrect. Slough is a soft film or stringy strands of dead material, not lumpy tissue that forms part of the wound wall.
Incorrect. Eschar is thick, dry, leathery black or brown dead tissue, not lumpy yellow tissue in the wound wall.
Incorrect. Purulent exudate is thick, opaque drainage that wipes away; it is not firm tissue in the wound wall.
questions.rationale: Yellow in a wound is not always dead tissue. Slough is soft, moist, stringy, or film-like nonviable material that covers the wound bed, and the RYB goal for it is to cleanse it away. Subcutaneous fat, which can be visible in a Stage 3 pressure injury, is living, lumpy tissue that forms part of the wound wall and must be protected. The tempting answer is slough because the tissue is yellow, but its texture and location identify it as living fat.
questions.takeaway: Yellow slough is a soft film or strands; lumpy yellow tissue in the wound wall is living fat.
questions.hintContent: Focus on the texture and location of the yellow tissue, not just its color.
questions.hintStrategy: When two look-alike findings share a color, use the other descriptors in the stem (texture, location, response to cleansing) to tell them apart.

questions.stem: A client with a Stage 3 sacral pressure injury containing yellow slough has a prescription for autolytic debridement. The client asks, “How is this dressing going to get rid of the dead tissue if nobody cuts it away?” Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: “The dressing contains a medicine that dissolves the dead tissue within a few hours.”
“The dressing dries onto the wound and then pulls the dead tissue off when we remove it later.”
“It holds in your wound's own fluid so your body's enzymes break down the dead tissue.”
“Tiny sterile larvae under the dressing eat away the dead tissue.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Applying a prescribed enzyme product describes chemical debridement, and autolytic debridement works slowly, not within hours.
Incorrect. A dressing that dries and pulls tissue off describes mechanical (wet-to-dry) debridement.

Correct. Autolytic debridement uses special dressings that capture and hold drainage so the body's own enzymes digest the dead tissue; the other responses describe chemical, mechanical, and biosurgical methods.
Incorrect. This accurately describes biosurgery (maggot therapy), another debridement method, but autolytic debridement relies on the body's own enzymes.
questions.rationale: Each debridement method removes dead tissue in a different way. Autolytic debridement uses special dressings that capture and hold the wound's own drainage, letting the body's enzymes break down the slough; it is the slowest and gentlest method. A prescribed enzyme ointment that dissolves dead tissue is chemical debridement, and a dressing that dries and pulls tissue away is mechanical debridement. The chemical description is the most tempting because both involve enzymes, but in autolytic debridement the enzymes come from the client's own body.
questions.takeaway: Autolytic debridement = special dressings that let the body's own enzymes break down dead tissue (slow and gentle).
questions.hintContent: Ask where the enzymes come from in autolytic debridement compared with chemical debridement.
questions.hintStrategy: For “accurate explanation” items, match each option to the method it actually describes and pick the one that matches the prescription.

questions.stem: A home health nurse reviews a caregiver's notes about a parent's sacral pressure injury, which has a mostly red, granulating wound bed. Which entry indicates the caregiver needs more teaching?
options: “I put the moist dressing over the red area the way the nurse showed me.”
“The red bumpy tissue bled a little, so I scrubbed it harder to get it clean.”
“I called the nurse when I saw a new black spot at the edge of the wound.”
“I kept turning Dad every 2 hours, even after the new dressing was started last week.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Keeping red granulation moist and covered matches the RYB goal to protect it.
Correct. Red granulation tissue is healthy and fragile; the goal is to protect it, and scrubbing damages the new tissue.
Incorrect. New black tissue means the wound may be deteriorating, so reporting it is correct.
Incorrect. Pressure relief must continue with any wound treatment, so this entry shows understanding.
questions.rationale: In the RYB guide, red means protect. Healthy granulation tissue is beefy red, moist, and bumpy, and it bleeds a little because it is full of new capillaries. Scrubbing it, especially harder because it bled, tears away the tissue that is filling the wound and shows the caregiver needs more teaching. The other entries reflect correct care: a moist protective dressing, reporting new black tissue, and continuing to turn the client.
questions.takeaway: Red granulation bleeds easily and is protected, never scrubbed.
questions.hintContent: Recall what slight bleeding from red, bumpy tissue means and the RYB goal for red tissue.
questions.hintStrategy: In “needs more teaching” items, look for the entry that would harm the client; the other choices describe correct care.

questions.stem: Refer to the Wound Assessment and Provider Orders for a client with two pressure injuries. Which prescription should the nurse clarify with the provider before implementing it?

rows: Stage 4; 100% beefy red, moist, bumpy granulation; scant serous drainage; no odor
Black eschar that is dry, intact, and firmly attached; no redness, swelling, bogginess, or drainage
Sacrum: wet-to-dry saline gauze every 6 hours
Right heel: keep eschar intact and dry; inspect each shift

options: Reposition the client every 2 hours
Heel-offloading boot while the client is in bed
Right heel: keep eschar intact and dry; inspect each shift
Sacrum: wet-to-dry saline gauze every 6 hours
optionRationales: Incorrect. Regular repositioning relieves pressure and is appropriate for any client with pressure injuries.
Incorrect. Offloading removes pressure from the heel and supports healing.
Incorrect. The heel eschar is dry, intact, firmly attached, and has no redness or drainage, so leaving it in place is appropriate.
Correct. The sacral wound is 100% red granulation; nonselective wet-to-dry gauze would tear away the healthy tissue the RYB guide says to protect.
questions.rationale: Each order should match the wound it treats. The sacral wound is 100% beefy red granulation with scant serous drainage, so the RYB goal is to protect it, yet the order is for wet-to-dry gauze, a nonselective method that strips healthy tissue and is meant for wounds with dead tissue to remove. The heel order is the tempting choice because the tissue is black, but the eschar is stable (dry, intact, firmly attached, no redness or drainage), so leaving it in place and offloading the heel is correct. The nurse clarifies the sacral order before carrying it out.
questions.takeaway: Clarify any wet-to-dry order for a clean, all-red wound; stable heel eschar is left intact.
questions.hintContent: Match each order to the RYB goal for the wound it targets, and remember the heel exception.
questions.hintStrategy: For “which order should be clarified,” check every order against the current assessment data; the order that would harm the tissue described is the one to question.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old client with a nonhealing Stage 4 heel wound full of necrotic tissue is scheduled for biosurgery. The client says, “The idea of maggots in my wound makes me sick. Will they eat my good tissue too?” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “That's a common worry. The sterile larvae eat dead tissue and do little harm to healthy tissue.”
“Many people feel this way at first. Would you like to talk more about your concerns?”
“Don't worry about that; your provider would never order anything that could hurt you.”
“The larvae are sterile and are raised in a lab especially for use in wound care.”
optionRationales: Correct. This acknowledges the client's feelings and gives accurate information: sterile larvae target necrotic tissue with minimal damage to healthy tissue.
Incorrect. This acknowledges the feeling and invites discussion, but it does not answer the client's direct question about healthy tissue.
Incorrect. This is false reassurance that dismisses the client's feelings and does not answer the question.
Incorrect. This is accurate, but it does not address the client's fear about healthy tissue or acknowledge the client's feelings.
questions.rationale: Clients are often uneasy about biosurgery, so the nurse acknowledges the feeling and then teaches accurately. Sterile maggots raised in a lab are placed on a nonhealing necrotic wound, where they digest dead tissue while doing minimal harm to healthy tissue. A therapeutic response validates the client's reaction and corrects the specific fear about losing healthy tissue. The reassurance option is tempting because it sounds kind, but it brushes off the client's concern and gives no information.
questions.takeaway: Biosurgery: sterile larvae digest dead tissue with minimal harm to healthy tissue; acknowledge the client's feelings, then teach.
questions.hintContent: Recall how selective maggot therapy is compared with wet-to-dry debridement.
questions.hintStrategy: For therapeutic communication, pick the option that both acknowledges the feeling and gives accurate information; eliminate false reassurance and misinformation.

questions.stem: The adult child of a client with a Stage 4 sacral pressure injury asks, “Why does all that dead tissue have to come off? Can't the wound just heal underneath it?” Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Removing it lets us see how deep the wound really is and measure it.”
“Dead tissue raises the risk of infection, so it needs to be removed.”
“New tissue grows up from the bottom, and dead tissue blocks it and feeds bacteria.”
“The new skin grows underneath the dead tissue, so removing it mainly helps reduce the odor.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This is a true benefit, but it does not explain why the wound cannot heal underneath the dead tissue.
Incorrect. This is true, but it is incomplete; it does not explain that dead tissue also blocks new tissue from filling the wound.
Correct. Dead tissue is a food source for bacteria, physically blocks granulation from filling the wound, and hides the wound's true depth.
Incorrect. New tissue cannot grow through necrotic tissue; removal is needed for healing, not just odor control.
questions.rationale: A pressure injury heals from the bottom up and from the edges in, so the wound bed must be clean and alive. Necrotic tissue gets in the way in three ways: it feeds bacteria, it physically blocks new granulation from growing, and it hides how deep the wound really is. That is why the RYB guide focuses on removing yellow slough and black eschar. The option about odor is tempting because necrotic wounds often smell, but odor control is a side benefit, not the reason debridement is needed.
questions.takeaway: Dead tissue feeds bacteria, blocks new tissue, and hides wound depth, so it must be removed for healing.
questions.hintContent: Picture how a pressure injury fills in, and what dead tissue does to that process.
questions.hintStrategy: For “most accurate explanation,” choose the option that states the underlying mechanism; eliminate options that give a minor or cosmetic reason.

questions.stem: Two days after the surgeon performed sharp debridement of a client's sacral pressure injury, the client's spouse says, “The wound is bigger and deeper than before. The surgery made it worse.” The wound bed is now 90% red granulation with no odor or purulent drainage. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “The surgeon may have removed too much tissue, so I'll report that the wound is worse.”
“The dead tissue was hiding the wound's real depth; the clean red base can now heal.”
“I can see this is upsetting. I'll ask the surgeon to come and explain it to you.”
“Wounds heal slowly, so I'll measure it each week to track how it is changing.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. A larger, deeper, mostly red wound after debridement is expected and does not indicate harm.
Correct. Necrotic tissue hides the true size and depth of a wound; once it is removed, the healthy red base can fill in from the bottom.
Incorrect. Acknowledging the concern is supportive, but the nurse can explain this expected finding now instead of deferring it.
Incorrect. Tracking the wound is appropriate, but this does not correct the spouse's belief that the surgery made the wound worse.
questions.rationale: Dead tissue hides how deep a wound really is. After sharp debridement removes the eschar, the wound often looks larger and deeper, but what the family is seeing is the true wound, now with a clean, red base that can heal. Today's findings, 90% red granulation with no odor or purulent drainage, show a wound ready to fill in, so the RYB goal is to protect it. Reporting the wound as “worse” is tempting because it looks bigger, but the size reflects what was hidden, not new damage.
questions.takeaway: A wound often looks larger after debridement because dead tissue was hiding its true depth.
questions.hintContent: Recall one of the three problems necrotic tissue causes, related to measuring the wound.
questions.hintStrategy: When a family member interprets a change as harm, compare the new findings with signs of true deterioration before agreeing or reassuring.

questions.stem: Refer to the Weekly Wound Assessment for a client with a Stage 4 sacral pressure injury who is receiving prescribed chemical (enzymatic) debridement. Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: The wound is deteriorating, because the yellow tissue increased during week 2
The treatment is not working, because the wound size stayed the same in week 2
Debridement can be stopped now, because the black eschar is completely gone
The wound is improving, because necrotic tissue is clearing and red tissue is increasing
optionRationales: Incorrect. The black eschar dropped from 50% to 20% in week 2; looking at yellow alone ignores the overall shift toward healthier tissue.
Incorrect. The size did stay the same in week 2, but tissue color shifted toward red, and the size decreased by week 3.
Incorrect. The black eschar is gone, but 20% yellow slough remains, so dead tissue still needs to be removed.
Correct. Black eschar fell from 50% to 0%, red granulation rose from 10% to 80%, and the size and drainage are decreasing.
questions.rationale: Evaluation means comparing data over time. In this record, black eschar fell from 50% to 0%, red granulation rose from 10% to 80%, the wound shrank, and drainage decreased with no odor, which is exactly the shift the RYB guide expects as debridement works. Yellow briefly increased in week 2, but overall necrotic tissue (black plus yellow) fell each week as red tissue grew. The week-2 yellow increase is the tempting trap; it has to be read along with the large drop in black eschar, not alone.
questions.takeaway: A debridement plan is working when black and yellow shrink and red grows over time.
questions.hintContent: Add up the nonviable tissue (black plus yellow) for each week and compare it with the red.
questions.hintStrategy: With trend data, judge the overall direction across all columns instead of fixing on one number that moved.

questions.stem: The RN is caring for a client with a Stage 4 sacral pressure injury that is being treated with a prescribed enzymatic debriding ointment. Which tasks can the RN delegate to the unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP)? Select all that apply.
options: Reposition the client every 2 hours using a lift sheet
Apply the enzymatic ointment to the black eschar
Tell the RN right away if the dressing is soiled or loose
Estimate the percentage of red, yellow, and black tissue
Record the percentage of each meal the client eats
Decide whether the wound shows signs of infection
optionRationales: Correct. Repositioning a stable client is routine care within the UAP's role and continues the pressure relief the wound needs.
Incorrect. Applying a prescribed debriding agent is a nursing treatment that requires assessment of the wound bed; it is not delegated to UAP.
Correct. Reporting an observation to the RN is within the UAP's role; the RN then assesses the wound.
Incorrect. Wound assessment requires nursing judgment and stays with the RN.
Correct. Measuring and recording intake is a routine task, and the RN uses the data to evaluate nutrition for healing.
Incorrect. Interpreting findings is assessment and cannot be delegated to UAP.
questions.rationale: UAP can perform routine, standardized tasks for stable clients, such as repositioning, recording intake, and reporting what they observe. Applying a prescribed debriding ointment, estimating red, yellow, and black percentages, and deciding whether a wound is infected all require nursing assessment and judgment, so the RN keeps them. Applying the ointment is the tempting choice because it looks like a simple skill, but it is a prescribed treatment that depends on the RN's assessment of where the necrotic tissue is. Pressure relief and nutrition still matter during debridement, which is why the UAP's tasks support healing.
questions.takeaway: Delegate routine care and reporting; keep wound assessment, interpretation, and prescribed debriding treatments with the RN.
questions.hintContent: Sort each task by whether it needs assessment or judgment, or is routine and standardized.
questions.hintStrategy: In delegation SATA, eliminate any task that involves assessing, interpreting, teaching, or applying a prescribed treatment that depends on assessment.

questions.stem: A client has a Stage 4 sacral pressure injury containing yellow slough and black eschar. Which findings should the nurse recognize as possible signs of wound infection? Select all that apply.
options: Beefy red tissue at one edge that bleeds slightly when touched
Wound pain that has increased over the past 2 days
Foul-smelling, thick, opaque drainage on the dressing
Redness and warmth spreading beyond the wound edge
A thin rim of new pink skin at the wound margin
WBC count rising from 9,000 to 16,400/mm³
optionRationales: Incorrect. This describes healthy granulation tissue, which is fragile and bleeds easily.
Correct. Increasing pain is an early sign of wound infection.
Correct. Purulent, foul-smelling drainage indicates infection.
Correct. Spreading redness and warmth suggest infection extending into surrounding tissue.
Incorrect. A pink rim is new epithelium, a sign of healing.
Correct. A rising WBC count supports a developing infection.
questions.rationale: Wounds that contain dead tissue are at higher risk for infection because necrotic tissue feeds bacteria. The nurse watches for increasing pain, spreading redness and warmth, purulent or foul-smelling drainage, fever, and a rising WBC, and reports them to the provider. Beefy red tissue that bleeds slightly and a pink rim of new skin are signs of healing, not infection. The bleeding granulation is the tempting distractor because “red” and “bleeding” sound worrisome, but fragile granulation is expected to bleed a little.
questions.takeaway: Infection cues: increasing pain, spreading redness and warmth, purulent or foul drainage, fever, rising WBC.
questions.hintContent: Separate signs of healthy healing tissue from signs that bacteria are winning.
questions.hintStrategy: In cue-recognition SATA, check each option on its own against the known sign list instead of guessing how many are correct.

questions.stem: After cleansing a client's pressure injury, the nurse is documenting the wound bed. Which findings should the nurse document as nonviable tissue? Select all that apply.
options: Soft, stringy yellow strands over part of the wound bed
A thick, dry, leathery black patch at one edge
A moist tan film covering part of the base
Beefy red, bumpy tissue that bleeds slightly
Lumpy yellow tissue forming part of the wound wall
A thin pink rim at the wound margins
optionRationales: Correct. Soft, stringy yellow material is slough, which is nonviable tissue.
Correct. Thick, dry, leathery black tissue is eschar, which is necrotic.
Correct. Slough can be yellow, cream, or tan and may form a film over the wound bed.
Incorrect. This is healthy granulation tissue, which is living and should be protected.
Incorrect. Lumpy yellow tissue in the wall is subcutaneous fat, which is living tissue, not slough.
Incorrect. A pink rim is new epithelium growing in from the edges.
questions.rationale: Nonviable tissue is dead tissue that cannot recover, and in the RYB guide it appears as yellow slough or black eschar. Slough is soft, moist, and stringy or film-like and may be yellow, cream, or tan; eschar is thick, dry, leathery, and black or dark brown. Beefy red granulation and a pink epithelial rim are living, healing tissue. Lumpy yellow fat is the trap: it is yellow, but it is living subcutaneous tissue that is part of the wound wall.
questions.takeaway: Slough (soft yellow or tan strands or film) and eschar (dry black leather) are nonviable; red granulation, pink epithelium, and fat are living.
questions.hintContent: Use texture and moisture, not just color, to decide whether each tissue is alive.
questions.hintStrategy: In classification SATA, test each option against the definition; watch for a look-alike that shares the color but not the other features.

questions.stem: A client's ischial pressure injury is 30% black eschar, 50% yellow slough, and 20% red granulation. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Scrub the red tissue firmly to remove any yellow film
Carry out the prescribed debridement of the black eschar first
Protect the red tissue from trauma and keep it moist
Limit sitting time and continue pressure relief off the ischium
Hold protein supplements until all dead tissue is removed
Leave the eschar in place as a natural protective cover
optionRationales: Incorrect. Scrubbing damages fragile granulation; slough is cleansed without traumatizing red tissue.
Correct. In a mixed wound, the least healthy tissue is addressed first: black, then yellow, then red.
Correct. Red granulation is healthy and fragile, so the goal is to protect it.
Correct. Debridement does not treat the cause; pressure relief must continue or the wound will not heal.
Incorrect. Nutrition supports healing throughout care and should not be delayed.
Incorrect. Only stable heel eschar is usually left in place; ischial eschar must be debrided for healing.
questions.rationale: In a mixed wound, the RYB guide works from the least healthy tissue to the healthiest: debride black, cleanse yellow, protect red. The nurse carries out the prescribed debridement of the eschar while protecting the red granulation from trauma and keeping it moist. Because debridement treats the wound, not the cause, pressure relief and nutrition continue throughout care. Leaving the eschar in place is tempting for students who remember the heel exception, but that exception applies only to stable heel eschar.
questions.takeaway: Mixed wound: black → yellow → red, while pressure relief and nutrition continue.
questions.hintContent: Assign an RYB goal to each color, then ask what else the wound needs that debridement cannot provide.
questions.hintStrategy: In plan-of-care SATA, include actions that match each finding and the underlying cause; eliminate actions that harm healthy tissue or pause basic care.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client and family about prescribed biosurgery (maggot therapy) for a nonhealing, necrotic Stage 4 sacral pressure injury. Which statements should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: “The larvae are raised in a lab so they are sterile.”
“The larvae stay in the wound until it has fully closed.”
“The larvae digest dead tissue and do little harm to healthy tissue.”
“Turning and pressure relief continue during the therapy.”
“Once the larvae are placed, no other wound care is needed.”
optionRationales: Correct. Biosurgery uses sterile larvae, so they do not bring germs into the wound.
Incorrect. The larvae are removed after the treatment period; they do not stay until the wound closes.
Correct. Biosurgery is selective; the larvae digest damaged tissue with minimal harm to surrounding healthy tissue.
Correct. Biosurgery removes dead tissue but does not treat the cause; pressure relief must continue.
Incorrect. The rest of the care plan, including pressure relief and nutrition, continues during biosurgery.
questions.rationale: Biosurgery places sterile, lab-raised larvae on a nonhealing wound that contains necrotic tissue. The larvae digest dead tissue while doing minimal harm to healthy tissue, and they are removed after treatment. Like every debridement method, biosurgery treats the wound, not the cause, so turning, support surfaces, and nutrition continue. The statement that no other care is needed is tempting to anxious families, but stopping pressure relief would undo the benefit of debridement.
questions.takeaway: Biosurgery: sterile larvae, selective for dead tissue, removed after treatment, and pressure relief continues.
questions.hintContent: Recall how selective maggot therapy is, and whether any debridement method replaces pressure relief.
questions.hintStrategy: In teaching SATA, include only statements that are accurate and keep the rest of the care plan intact.

questions.stem: A provider has prescribed wet-to-dry saline gauze dressings for several clients' wounds. For which wounds should the nurse clarify the prescription before carrying it out? Select all that apply.
options: A coccyx wound covered with 80% soft, stringy yellow slough
A sacral wound that is 100% beefy red, moist granulation
A trochanter wound with red granulation and a new pink rim at the edges
A sacral wound that is 50% loose, moist necrotic tissue and 50% slough
A clean incision that is sutured closed and healing by primary intention
optionRationales: Incorrect. This wound contains nonviable tissue, so mechanical debridement is a reasonable choice.
Correct. Wet-to-dry is nonselective and would tear away healthy granulation that should be protected.
Correct. Red tissue and new epithelium are signs of healing that need protection, not nonselective debridement.
Incorrect. A wound full of dead tissue is an appropriate target for mechanical debridement.
Correct. A closed incision has no dead tissue to remove, so a debriding dressing does not fit the wound.
questions.rationale: Wet-to-dry gauze dries onto the wound bed and pulls off whatever it touches when removed, so it is nonselective and painful. It belongs only in wounds that contain dead tissue to remove, such as wounds with slough or necrotic tissue. Clean red granulation, new pink epithelium, and a closed incision have no nonviable tissue, so a wet-to-dry order would cause harm and should be clarified. The slough-filled wounds are the tempting picks because they look the worst, but those are exactly the wounds mechanical debridement is meant for.
questions.takeaway: Wet-to-dry belongs in wounds with dead tissue; clarify it for clean red, epithelializing, or closed wounds.
questions.hintContent: For each wound, ask whether there is any dead tissue for the gauze to remove.
questions.hintStrategy: When asked which orders to clarify, compare each order with the specific tissue described; question the ones that would damage healthy tissue.

questions.stem: Refer to the Wound Infection Trend for a client with an infected Stage 4 sacral pressure injury. A wound culture was obtained, and prescribed IV antibiotics were started on day 1. Which findings indicate the treatment is effective? Select all that apply.

rows: 3 cm past wound edge; outlined with skin marker

options: The redness now lies inside the line drawn with a skin marker on day 1
The temperature has fallen from 38.8 °C to 37.1 °C
Every antibiotic dose has been given on schedule
The drainage has changed from foul and purulent to scant and serous
The WBC count has fallen from 17,200 to 10,400/mm³
The client says the wound feels the same as before
optionRationales: Correct. Redness receding inside the marked border is a measurable sign that the infection is improving.
Correct. A falling temperature trend shows the body's response to infection is settling.
Incorrect. On-time doses show the treatment was given, not that it worked.
Correct. Drainage changing from purulent to serous shows the infection is resolving.
Correct. A falling WBC count toward normal supports improvement.
Incorrect. Unchanged pain does not show improvement; infection-related pain should be decreasing.
questions.rationale: To evaluate treatment of an infected wound, the nurse compares current data with the baseline. Redness that has receded inside the line drawn on day 1, a falling temperature, a falling WBC count, and drainage that has changed from purulent to serous all show measurable improvement. Giving every dose on time is the tempting choice because it reflects good nursing care, but it shows the treatment was delivered, not that it worked. Pain that has not changed is not evidence of improvement.
questions.takeaway: Judge infection treatment by outcomes (redness border, temperature, WBC, drainage), not by doses given.
questions.hintContent: Look for data that moved from the day-1 baseline toward normal.
questions.hintStrategy: In evaluate-outcome SATA, eliminate options that describe the process of care rather than a change in the client.

questions.stem: A client's heel pressure injury is covered by black eschar that has been left in place because it was stable. Which new findings indicate the eschar is no longer stable and should be reported to the provider? Select all that apply.
options: The eschar is dry and firmly attached to the heel
The eschar now feels soft and boggy
Cloudy drainage is seeping from under the eschar's edge
Redness and swelling now surround the eschar
The skin around the heel is intact with no warmth
The eschar is dark brown instead of black
optionRationales: Incorrect. Dry, firmly attached eschar is a feature of stable eschar.
Correct. Softening or bogginess means the eschar is no longer a stable, protective cover.
Correct. Drainage from under eschar suggests it is breaking down and may be infected.
Correct. New redness and swelling around the edges suggest inflammation or infection under the eschar.
Incorrect. Intact surrounding skin without warmth is consistent with stable eschar.
Incorrect. Eschar may be black or dark brown; color alone does not mean it has become unstable.
questions.rationale: Stable heel eschar is dry, intact, firmly attached, and free of redness, swelling, bogginess, and drainage; it is usually left in place as a natural cover. When the eschar becomes soft or boggy, starts draining, or develops redness and swelling around its edges, it is no longer protecting the heel and may be hiding an infection. These changes are reported to the provider so the plan can be revised. Dark brown color is the distractor most likely to fool students, but eschar can be black or dark brown, so color alone does not signal instability.
questions.takeaway: Report heel eschar that becomes soft, boggy, draining, or surrounded by redness and swelling.
questions.hintContent: List the features that make heel eschar stable, then look for findings that break those features.
questions.hintStrategy: When a finding is safe only under certain conditions, choose the options that show those conditions are no longer met.

questions.stem: Refer to the Hand-off Report. Which client should the nurse assess first?

rows: 45 years old; POD 1 after laparoscopic cholecystectomy
Mild redness at port sites; small amount of serosanguineous drainage; pain 3/10
81 years old; POD 4 after hip repair
New agitation overnight; temp 37.7 °C (baseline 36.4 °C); ate 20% of meals today; incision newly warm and firm
33 years old; POD 8 after cesarean birth
Incision itchy; firm ridge palpable under incision; afebrile
60 years old; day 12 of open leg wound
Beefy red, moist, bumpy tissue that bled slightly during dressing change

options: Client 2: POD 4 after hip repair, 81 years old
Client 1: POD 1 after laparoscopic cholecystectomy
Client 3: POD 8 after cesarean birth
Client 4: day 12 of an open leg wound
optionRationales: Correct. New agitation, a temperature above the client's own baseline, poor intake, and a newly warm, firm incision are early infection cues in an older adult, whose blunted immune response often hides a high fever.
Incorrect. Mild redness and a small amount of serosanguineous drainage on POD 1 are expected inflammatory-phase findings.
Incorrect. Itching and a firm palpable ridge on POD 8 are expected proliferative-phase findings.
Incorrect. Beefy red tissue that bleeds slightly is healthy granulation and is expected.
questions.rationale: Older adults heal more slowly and more quietly, and infection often shows up first as new confusion or agitation, a small temperature rise above the client's own baseline, loss of appetite, or functional decline rather than a high fever. Client 2 has several of these cues together, plus a newly warm, firm incision, so this client needs assessment first. The other three clients show expected findings for their phase of healing. The 37.7 °C temperature can look harmless, which is the trap; compared with a baseline of 36.4 °C it is a meaningful rise.
questions.takeaway: In older adults, new confusion, a temperature above personal baseline, and poor intake can be the first signs of wound infection.
questions.hintContent: Compare each temperature with the client's own baseline and look for behavior changes in the oldest client.

questions.stem: An unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP) is about to move a 90-year-old client up in bed. The client is on POD 3 after hip repair and has thin, fragile skin. Which instruction by the RN is most important?
options: “Have the client push with the heels to help slide up toward the head of the bed.”
“Raise the bed to your waist height before you move the client.”
“Use a draw sheet and a second helper to lift rather than slide.”
“Check the skin on the hips and sacrum after you finish the move.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Pushing with the heels drags the skin and heels against the sheets, creating friction and shear.
Incorrect. Good body mechanics protect the UAP, but this does not prevent the shear that tears fragile skin.
Correct. Older adults have thin, fragile skin that tears easily, so the client is lifted with a draw sheet rather than dragged.
Incorrect. Checking skin is appropriate, but it finds damage after it happens; lifting instead of sliding prevents it.
questions.rationale: With aging, skin becomes thinner and more fragile with less fat and fewer blood vessels underneath, so it tears easily. The safest way to move a frail older adult is to lift with a draw sheet and enough help, never to drag the client across the sheets. A skin tear is a new wound, not an expected finding, and it adds to the healing burden of a client who already heals slowly. Having the client push with the heels is tempting because it seems to involve the client, but it creates friction and shear on fragile skin.
questions.takeaway: Lift fragile older adults with a draw sheet; don't drag.
questions.hintContent: Think about how aging changes the skin's layers and what happens when fragile skin is dragged.
questions.hintStrategy: For delegation instructions, pick the one that prevents the most likely injury for this specific client.

questions.stem: Four clients are being cared for on a surgical unit. Based on how each wound is closing, which client is at greatest risk for wound infection?
options: A client whose incision is sutured closed with edges approximated
A client whose large open wound is filling in with granulation
A client whose contaminated wound was closed after 4 days open
A client whose laceration was closed with skin adhesive
optionRationales: Incorrect. A wound healing by primary intention has the lowest infection risk because its edges are closed.
Correct. Secondary intention leaves the wound open to the environment for a long time, giving it the highest infection risk.
Incorrect. Tertiary intention carries moderate risk; the wound was closed once swelling and contamination resolved.
Incorrect. Skin adhesive approximates the edges, so this is also primary intention with low infection risk.
questions.rationale: The way a wound closes affects its infection risk. Primary intention wounds have approximated edges and the lowest risk. Tertiary (delayed primary) wounds are open for about 3–5 days and then closed, so the risk is moderate. Secondary intention wounds have extensive tissue loss, stay open while they fill in from the bottom, and are exposed to the environment longest, so they carry the highest risk. The contaminated wound is the tempting choice because “contaminated” sounds dangerous, but it was closed after the contamination cleared.
questions.takeaway: Secondary intention (open, filling from the bottom) has the highest infection risk; primary has the lowest.
questions.hintContent: Ask which wound stays open to the environment the longest.
questions.hintStrategy: When options describe different wound types, rank them by the feature the stem asks about, not by the most alarming word.

questions.stem: During a prescribed dressing change on a client's open abdominal wound that is healing by secondary intention, the beefy red, moist, bumpy wound bed bleeds slightly as the nonadherent dressing is lifted. Vital signs are unchanged from baseline. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Stop the dressing change and call the surgeon to report hemorrhage
Recheck the vital signs before continuing the dressing change
Document the bleeding and report it at the next provider round
Apply gentle pressure, finish the change, and document the finding
optionRationales: Incorrect. Slight bleeding from granulation with stable vital signs is expected, not hemorrhage.
Incorrect. Vital signs are already stable, and slight oozing from granulation is expected, so rechecking delays the care the client needs.
Incorrect. Documenting is needed, but this does not control the oozing, and slight bleeding from granulation does not need to be reported.
Correct. Healthy granulation is packed with new capillaries and bleeds easily; gentle pressure controls the oozing, and the finding is documented.
questions.rationale: In the proliferative phase, granulation tissue fills an open wound. Healthy granulation is beefy red, moist, and bumpy, and because it is full of fragile new capillaries it bleeds slightly when touched. With stable vital signs, slight oozing is expected; the nurse applies gentle pressure, protects the tissue, completes the prescribed change, and documents. Calling the surgeon for hemorrhage is the tempting overreaction, since true hemorrhage involves heavy bleeding or changing vital signs.
questions.takeaway: Healthy granulation bleeds slightly when touched; protect it and document.
questions.hintContent: Identify the tissue first, then decide whether slight bleeding from it is expected.
questions.hintStrategy: Before choosing an emergency action, check whether the stem's vital signs and amount support an emergency.

questions.stem: A client is on POD 2 after an open inguinal hernia repair. The incision edges are approximated, with a 0.5-cm band of mild redness and slight swelling along the sutures. The area is slightly warm, and there is a scant amount of clear, watery drainage on the dressing. Temperature is 37.3 °C (99.1 °F). The client asks, “Is it infected?” Which action should the nurse take?
options: Explain these are expected early healing findings and keep monitoring
Notify the surgeon that the incision shows signs of infection
Obtain a culture of the clear drainage before the next dressing change
Recheck the temperature in 1 hour before answering the client
optionRationales: Correct. Redness, edema, slight warmth, and exudate are normal signs of the inflammatory phase in the first days after surgery.
Incorrect. Watching for infection is important, but mild redness, swelling, warmth, and serous drainage on POD 2 are expected inflammatory-phase findings, not infection.
Incorrect. A culture is not indicated for expected serous drainage without signs of infection.
Incorrect. Monitoring temperature is reasonable, but the current data already show expected findings, and the client's question can be answered now.
questions.rationale: The inflammatory phase lasts about 3–6 days after injury. Blood vessels near the wound widen and leak so white blood cells can enter, which causes mild redness, edema, warmth, and exudate. These are normal early signs, so on POD 2 the nurse explains them, documents, and continues monitoring. Notifying the surgeon is tempting because the findings resemble infection, but infection usually shows up around POD 3–5 as increasing pain, spreading redness, and purulent drainage.
questions.takeaway: Mild redness, swelling, warmth, and serous drainage in the first days after surgery are expected inflammation.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old client is on POD 4 after repair of a wrist fracture. The client is alert, oriented, eating well, and at baseline temperature. The client's daughter says, “Mom's incision barely looks red or swollen, and it's closing slower than mine did. Is something wrong?” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “A weak response like this means an infection is hiding, so I'll ask for a culture.”
“Healing slows with age, but I'll notify the surgeon so the incision can be checked.”
“Older adults often have a milder inflammatory response and close wounds more slowly.”
“Extra protein in her diet will help the incision heal faster, so let's work on that.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. There are no infection cues such as new confusion, a temperature above baseline, or poor intake.
Incorrect. The first part is accurate, but there are no abnormal findings, so notifying the surgeon is unnecessary.
Correct. Aging slows and weakens the inflammatory response and epithelialization, so less redness and slower closure are expected.
Incorrect. Protein supports healing, but the client is eating well, and this does not answer whether something is wrong.
questions.rationale: Older adults can heal well, but more slowly and more quietly. Aging brings thinner skin with fewer blood vessels, a slower and weaker inflammatory response, and slower epithelialization, so an incision may look less red and swollen and take longer to close. Because this client is alert, eating well, and at baseline temperature, these are expected age-related changes. The “hidden infection” option is tempting because blunted inflammation can mask infection, but there are no infection cues here to act on.
questions.takeaway: Less redness and slower closure in an older adult are expected; new confusion or a temperature above baseline is not.
questions.hintContent: Recall how aging changes the inflammatory phase, and check the stem for any actual infection cues.
questions.hintStrategy: For a best-response item, choose the accurate teaching that fits the data; don't escalate when the stem rules out the complication.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old warehouse worker is 3 weeks after an open inguinal hernia repair. The incision is closed and well approximated. The client says, “It looks healed, so I'm going back to lifting heavy boxes tomorrow.” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Avoid heavy lifting until the incision no longer feels sore when you touch it.”
“The scar keeps gaining strength for months, so follow your surgeon's lifting limits.”
“Start with lighter boxes tomorrow and add weight as long as you have no pain.”
“Lifting is fine as long as you wear an abdominal binder while you are working.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Limiting lifting is right, but lack of tenderness does not mean the scar is strong; the surgeon's limits guide when to resume.
Correct. Maturation starts around day 21 and lasts 1–2 years; the scar is still gaining strength and never fully matches the original tissue.
Incorrect. Gradual activity sounds cautious, but pain is not a reliable guide to scar strength, and the surgeon's limits still apply.
Incorrect. A binder does not replace the surgeon's lifting restrictions while the scar is still gaining strength.
questions.rationale: By about day 21 the wound is entering the maturation phase, when collagen reorganizes into a stronger pattern. This phase lasts 1–2 years, and even a fully mature scar reaches only about 70–80% of the original tissue's strength. A wound that looks closed on the surface is still weak underneath, so heavy lifting should wait for the surgeon's clearance. The binder option is tempting because it sounds protective, but it does not make an immature scar strong enough for heavy loads.
questions.takeaway: A closed incision is not a strong incision; scars keep maturing for 1–2 years and never regain full strength.
questions.hintContent: Place 3 weeks on the healing timeline and recall how strong a scar ever becomes.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options with absolute claims about strength (“as strong,” “stronger”); choose the accurate, safety-focused teaching.

questions.stem: The nurse assesses four open wounds that are healing by secondary intention. Which finding requires the nurse's priority follow-up?
options: Beefy red, bumpy tissue that bleeds slightly in a 2-week-old wound
A thin pink rim of new skin at the margins of a sacral wound
A wound that is smaller and shallower than it was last week
Pale, dry, dusky tissue at the base of a 3-week-old leg wound
optionRationales: Incorrect. This is healthy granulation tissue from the proliferative phase.
Incorrect. A pink rim shows epithelial cells migrating in from the edges, which is expected.
Incorrect. A shrinking, shallower wound shows healing is progressing.
Correct. Pale, dry, or dusky tissue suggests poor blood supply and poor healing, so it needs follow-up.
questions.rationale: Healthy granulation is beefy red, moist, and bumpy because it is full of new capillaries. When granulation looks pale, dry, or dusky, the wound is not getting enough blood flow, oxygen, and nutrients, and healing is stalling. That finding needs follow-up, including assessment of circulation and other factors and a report to the provider. The bleeding granulation is the tempting answer, but slight bleeding is a sign of healthy, well-perfused tissue.
questions.takeaway: Beefy red, moist granulation is healthy; pale, dry, or dusky tissue signals poor blood supply.
questions.hintContent: Think about what the color of granulation tells you about blood flow to the wound.
questions.hintStrategy: When three options describe signs of progress, the odd one out that suggests poor perfusion is the priority.

questions.stem: Refer to the Incision Assessment Record for a client who had an open colectomy with a sutured midline incision. Which entry is the first to show a finding that is NOT expected for normal healing?

rows: Edges approximated; mild redness and edema along sutures
Redness spreading 2 cm from incision; pain increased since yesterday
Redness 4 cm from incision; incision warm and indurated

options: POD 5
POD 3
POD 1
POD 7
optionRationales: Correct. Redness spreading 2 cm from the incision, increasing pain, and thick yellow drainage on POD 5 suggest infection rather than normal inflammation.
Incorrect. Fading redness and scant serous drainage show inflammation settling as expected.
Incorrect. Mild redness and edema with scant serosanguineous drainage are expected in the inflammatory phase.
Incorrect. POD 7 still shows the infection that began on POD 5, so it is not the first unexpected entry.
questions.rationale: Normal inflammation peaks early and then fades: mild redness, swelling, and serous or serosanguineous drainage in the first days are expected. By POD 3 the redness should be fading and the drainage clear and scant. On POD 5 the course reverses, with spreading redness, increasing pain, and thick yellow drainage, which is the typical timing and picture of wound infection. POD 7 is tempting because its findings are clearly abnormal, but the question asks for the first entry that breaks the expected pattern.
questions.takeaway: Redness and drainage should fade after the first days; spreading redness, more pain, and purulent drainage around POD 3–5 suggest infection.

questions.stem: A client with a sutured hand laceration asks the nurse, “What is my body doing to clean out the wound during the first few days?” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Macrophages arrive first, and then neutrophils lay down collagen to close the gap.”
“Fibroblasts clear out the bacteria first, and then platelets build new tissue.”
“Neutrophils eat bacteria first; then macrophages clear debris and signal rebuilding.”
“Collagen fibers trap the bacteria, and then skin cells digest the debris.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Neutrophils arrive before macrophages, and collagen is made by fibroblasts in the proliferative phase.
Incorrect. Fibroblasts make collagen, and platelets form the clot; neither clears bacteria.
Correct. In the inflammatory phase, neutrophils arrive first, and macrophages follow to finish the cleanup and signal the start of rebuilding.
Incorrect. Collagen gives strength in the proliferative phase; white blood cells clean the wound.
questions.rationale: The inflammatory phase has two jobs: stop the bleeding and clean the wound. After hemostasis, nearby blood vessels widen and leak so white blood cells can reach the tissue. Neutrophils arrive first and eat bacteria; macrophages follow, clear dead tissue and debris, and release signals that start the proliferative (rebuilding) phase. The option with macrophages first is tempting because it names the right cells, but it reverses their order and assigns collagen to the wrong cell.
questions.takeaway: Inflammatory cleanup order: neutrophils first, then macrophages, which also signal rebuilding.
questions.hintContent: Recall which white blood cell arrives first and which one starts the rebuilding phase.
questions.hintStrategy: When options use the same terms in different orders, check the sequence and each cell's job carefully.

questions.stem: Eight weeks after a thyroidectomy, a client notices that the neck scar is thick, raised, and red but stays within the borders of the original incision. The client asks, “Is this a keloid?” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Yes. Any raised scar is a keloid, and it will keep growing larger over time.”
“If it stays inside the incision edges, it's a hypertrophic scar, which often flattens.”
“Keloids are more common in people with darker skin, so it depends on your skin tone.”
“It's too early to tell; a keloid can't be identified until the scar is a year old.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. A keloid extends beyond the original wound edges; a raised scar within the borders is not a keloid.
Correct. A hypertrophic scar is thick and raised but stays within the original wound borders and often flattens over time.
Incorrect. Keloids are more common in darker skin, but skin tone does not tell the scar types apart; the scar's borders do.
Incorrect. Waiting and watching a new scar is reasonable, but a keloid is identified by growth beyond the wound edges, not by age; this scar stays within its borders, so it is hypertrophic.
questions.rationale: Both hypertrophic scars and keloids come from too much collagen during maturation, but they differ in one key way. A hypertrophic scar is thick and raised yet stays within the borders of the original wound, and it often flattens over time. A keloid extends beyond the original wound edges and can be shiny, raised, and itchy; it is more common in people with darker skin. Agreeing that it is a keloid is tempting because both scars are raised, but the scar's borders are what tell them apart.
questions.takeaway: Hypertrophic scar stays within the wound borders; a keloid grows beyond them.
questions.hintContent: Look at where the scar's edges are compared with the original incision.
questions.hintStrategy: For look-alike conditions, find the single feature in the stem that separates them.

questions.stem: Three months after a total knee replacement, a client says, “My scar is still pinkish-purple and a little raised. Did it heal wrong?” The incision is closed, with no drainage, warmth, or tenderness. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “A scar should be flat and pale by 6 weeks, so I'll let your surgeon know.”
“Gently massaging the scar each day may help it soften and flatten over time.”
“Keeping the scar out of the sun will help it fade, so use sunscreen on it.”
“Scars keep remodeling for 1 to 2 years and usually flatten and fade with time.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Maturation lasts 1–2 years, so a scar is not expected to be flat and pale by 6 weeks.
Incorrect. Scar massage may help, but this does not answer whether the scar healed wrong or explain the expected timeline.
Incorrect. Sun protection is good advice, but it does not explain that this appearance is expected during maturation.
Correct. During maturation, collagen reorganizes and the scar slowly flattens and fades from red or purple to paler than the surrounding skin.
questions.rationale: The maturation (remodeling) phase starts around day 21 and lasts 1–2 years. During this time, collagen reorganizes, and the scar slowly strengthens, flattens, and fades from red or purple to paler than the surrounding skin. At 3 months, with no drainage, warmth, or tenderness, a pinkish-purple, slightly raised scar is expected. Notifying the surgeon is tempting for a cautious nurse, but it is based on the wrong timeline.
questions.takeaway: Scars keep flattening and fading for 1–2 years during maturation.
questions.hintContent: Place 3 months on the healing timeline and recall how long the last phase lasts.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old's chin laceration is cleaned and closed with skin adhesive in the emergency department. The parent asks, “Will this leave a big scar?” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “The edges are held together, so it heals by primary intention with minimal scarring.”
“Glue leaves the cut partly open, so it fills in from the bottom and scars more.”
“Every wound leaves some scar, so it's too early to say how this one will look.”
“Keeping the area out of the sun as it heals will help the scar fade over time.”
optionRationales: Correct. Adhesive approximates the edges, so the wound heals by primary intention with minimal granulation and minimal scarring.
Incorrect. Skin adhesive holds the edges together; filling in from the bottom describes secondary intention.
Incorrect. Some scarring is expected, but the nurse can explain that edges held together heal by primary intention with minimal scarring.
Incorrect. Sun protection is helpful, but it does not answer how much scarring to expect from this closure.
questions.rationale: Primary intention occurs when wound edges are approximated, whether with sutures, staples, or adhesive closure such as skin glue. Because little tissue is lost and only a thin line needs to heal, there is minimal granulation and minimal scarring. Secondary intention applies to open wounds with extensive tissue loss, and tertiary intention applies to wounds left open for about 3–5 days before closure. The “glue leaves it open” option is tempting for parents who expect stitches, but adhesive closes the edges just as sutures do.
questions.takeaway: Edges held together by sutures, staples, or adhesive = primary intention with minimal scarring.
questions.hintContent: Decide whether the edges of this wound are approximated, and how.
questions.hintStrategy: Classify the wound first (primary, secondary, tertiary), then choose the statement that matches that type.

questions.stem: A nursing student palpates a client's sutured abdominal incision on POD 3 and reports, “I can't feel a healing ridge. Should we call the surgeon?” The edges are approximated with mild redness and no drainage. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “No ridge means collagen formation has failed, so the incision may open later today.”
“Check again tomorrow, and call the surgeon if the ridge is still missing then.”
“A ridge is usually felt by about the end of the first week, so this is expected.”
“A ridge isn't needed to judge healing; just check that the edges stay closed.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Collagen is only beginning to form on POD 3; a missing ridge is a concern near the end of the first week, not now.
Incorrect. Rechecking is reasonable, but a ridge is not expected by POD 4 either; a missing ridge becomes a concern near POD 9.
Correct. The healing ridge forms from new collagen during the proliferative phase and is usually palpable by about the end of the first week.
Incorrect. Checking the edges is appropriate, but the healing ridge is a key sign of collagen formation and should be felt by the end of the first week.
questions.rationale: A healing ridge is a firm ridge under a closed incision made by new collagen. Fibroblasts begin laying down collagen in the proliferative phase, starting around day 3, and the ridge is usually palpable by about the end of the first week. On POD 3, its absence is expected, while a missing ridge around POD 9 would signal inadequate collagen and a higher risk of dehiscence. The tempting answer warns of imminent opening, but it applies the POD 9 rule too early.
questions.takeaway: No healing ridge is expected on POD 3; no ridge by about POD 9 is a warning sign.
questions.hintContent: Recall when collagen production starts and when a ridge is usually palpable.
