questions.stem: During a preoperative interview, a 30-year-old client of Asian descent who is scheduled for elective abdominal surgery mentions having “bad scars.” Which question by the nurse is most important to help the team plan for scarring problems?
options: “Have any of your scars been thick and raised but stayed inside the cut?”
“Have you ever had a scar grow beyond the edges of the original cut?”
“Have any of your scars ever itched while they were healing?”
“Did any of your past incisions become infected while they were healing?”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This identifies a hypertrophic scar, which is useful, but it does not identify a keloid, the main concern for this client.
Correct. A scar that extends beyond the original wound edges is a keloid; a history of keloids should be shared with the surgeon so prevention can be planned.
Incorrect. Itching is common during healing and does not distinguish a keloid from a normal scar.
Incorrect. Past infection is useful healing history, but it does not assess the client's tendency to form problem scars.
questions.rationale: A keloid is an overgrown scar that extends beyond the original wound edges, and keloids are more common in people with darker skin, including people of African and Asian descent. A client who has had a keloid before should tell the surgeon before any new surgery so prevention can be planned. The most useful question therefore asks specifically whether a scar has grown past the original wound edges, which separates a keloid from a hypertrophic or normal scar. The itching question is tempting because keloids can itch, but many normal healing scars itch too.
questions.takeaway: Ask whether a scar ever grew beyond the original wound edges; a keloid history should be shared with the surgeon.
questions.hintContent: Identify the single feature that defines a keloid and turn it into a question.

questions.stem: On POD 7 after an open appendectomy, a client touches the incision and says, “There's a hard ridge under my scar. Should I rub it to break it up?” The incision is closed and dry, with no redness or warmth. Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “That lump should be checked, so I'll let your surgeon know today.”
“Don't rub it, but call your surgeon if it gets red or starts to drain.”
“Gentle scar massage can help later, once the incision has fully healed.”
“That firm ridge is new collagen, a good sign of healing, so leave it alone.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Reporting a new lump is a cautious instinct, but there is no redness, warmth, or drainage, and a firm ridge on POD 7 is expected healing that needs no report.
Incorrect. Advising against rubbing and teaching warning signs are both appropriate, but this response never tells the client what the ridge is or that it is a good sign, so it is incomplete.
Incorrect. Scar massage is sometimes used after full healing, but it is mistimed advice that does not explain the ridge the client is worried about now.
Correct. A healing ridge forms from new collagen and is usually felt by about the end of the first week; it is a sign of healing.
questions.rationale: During the proliferative phase, fibroblasts lay down collagen, and in a closed incision this forms a firm healing ridge that is usually palpable by about the end of the first week. The ridge is a good sign: it means the incision is gaining strength. The client should be reassured and taught not to disrupt it. Notifying the surgeon is tempting because the client describes a hard lump, but there is no redness, warmth, or drainage to suggest a problem, and a healing ridge is expected.
questions.takeaway: A firm ridge under an incision around the end of the first week is healing collagen, a good sign.
questions.hintContent: Recall what forms under a closed incision during the first week and what it means.

questions.stem: A client's sacral pressure injury is healing by secondary intention. The client says, “My surgery incision last year healed in a couple of weeks. Why is this one taking so long?” Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “This wound has to fill in with new tissue from the bottom up before skin covers it.”
“Your body is closing this wound with collagen only, so it skips the inflammatory phase.”
“It is healing by primary intention, which always takes longer than an incision.”
“The wound is slow because it was closed late, after it was left open for several days.”
optionRationales: Correct. With extensive tissue loss and edges that cannot be brought together, the body must build a large amount of granulation tissue before skin grows across.
Incorrect. All wounds go through the inflammatory phase; skipping it would not slow healing.
Incorrect. Primary intention is the fastest type of healing and requires approximated edges.
Incorrect. A wound left open and closed later is tertiary intention; this wound is staying open.
questions.rationale: A surgical incision heals by primary intention: its edges are approximated, little tissue is lost, and only a thin line needs to heal. A pressure injury heals by secondary intention because the tissue loss is extensive and the edges cannot be brought together. It must fill in slowly from the bottom and sides with granulation tissue before skin grows across, so it takes longer, scars more, and carries a higher infection risk. The “closed late” option is tempting because it explains a delay, but that describes tertiary intention.
questions.takeaway: Secondary intention fills from the bottom up, so it heals more slowly and scars more than primary intention.
questions.hintContent: Compare how much tissue each wound has to rebuild and whether its edges can be brought together.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the wounds of several clients on a surgical unit. Which wounds are healing by secondary intention? Select all that apply.
options: A drained abscess cavity left open and packed so it fills in on its own
A laparoscopic port incision closed with skin adhesive
A Stage 4 sacral pressure injury with extensive tissue loss
A contaminated abdominal wound that was left open for 4 days and then sutured
A deep leg wound from a crash with edges too far apart to be brought together
A knee incision closed with staples
optionRationales: Correct. A wound left open to fill in from the bottom heals by secondary intention.
Incorrect. Adhesive approximates the edges, so this heals by primary intention.
Correct. A pressure injury with extensive tissue loss cannot be approximated and heals by secondary intention.
Incorrect. A wound left open for a few days and then closed heals by tertiary (delayed primary) intention.
Correct. When tissue loss prevents approximation, the wound stays open and heals by secondary intention.
Incorrect. Staples approximate the edges, so this heals by primary intention.
questions.rationale: The type of intention depends on what happens to the wound edges. Primary intention wounds are approximated with sutures, staples, or adhesive. Secondary intention wounds have extensive tissue loss and are left open to fill in from the bottom with granulation tissue, as with pressure injuries, packed abscess cavities, and wounds whose edges cannot be brought together. The contaminated wound closed on day 4 is the tempting distractor because it was open for a while, but being closed later makes it tertiary intention.
questions.takeaway: Left open to fill in from the bottom = secondary; closed right away = primary; open first, closed later = tertiary.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a new graduate how to evaluate the wound bed of an open wound healing by secondary intention. Which findings indicate healthy granulation tissue? Select all that apply.
options: Pale pink, dry tissue
Beefy red color
A moist surface
A bumpy, granular texture
Slight bleeding when touched
Dusky, grayish color
optionRationales: Incorrect. Pale or dry tissue suggests poor blood supply and poor healing.
Correct. Healthy granulation is beefy red because it is packed with new capillaries.
Correct. Healthy granulation is moist.
Correct. Granulation has a bumpy, granular (cobblestone) texture.
Correct. Fragile new capillaries make healthy granulation bleed easily.
Incorrect. Dusky tissue signals poor perfusion, not healthy granulation.
questions.rationale: During the proliferative phase, new tiny blood vessels grow into the wound and combine with collagen to form granulation tissue. Healthy granulation is beefy red, moist, and bumpy, and it bleeds easily because of its fragile new capillaries. Pale, dry, or dusky tissue suggests the wound is not getting enough blood flow and healing is poor. Slight bleeding is the option students most often leave out, because bleeding sounds abnormal, but it is a hallmark of well-perfused granulation.
questions.takeaway: Healthy granulation is beefy red, moist, bumpy, and bleeds easily; pale, dry, or dusky tissue signals poor healing.

questions.stem: An 87-year-old client is on POD 3 after repair of a hip fracture. Which actions by the nurse reflect age-related differences in wound healing? Select all that apply.
options: Compare each temperature with the client's own baseline
Report new confusion or agitation as a possible sign of infection
Use a draw sheet to lift the client rather than sliding the client
Rely on a high fever as the main sign of wound infection
Request a wound culture because the incision is closing slowly
Monitor appetite and willingness to do therapy each shift
optionRationales: Correct. Older adults often do not run a high fever, so a small rise above personal baseline can be an infection cue.
Correct. In older adults, infection may first appear as new confusion or agitation.
Correct. Thin, fragile skin tears easily, so the client is lifted, not dragged.
Incorrect. The blunted immune response in older adults often prevents a high fever.
Incorrect. Slower closure is an expected age-related change, not a reason for a culture by itself.
Correct. Loss of appetite and refusing therapy or functional decline can be early infection cues in older adults.
questions.rationale: Older adults heal more slowly and more quietly because the inflammatory response is slower and weaker and the skin is thinner and more fragile. Infection may not cause a high fever; it may appear first as new confusion, a small temperature rise above the client's own baseline, poor appetite, or refusing therapy. The nurse watches for those cues and lifts the client with a draw sheet to prevent skin tears. Requesting a culture for slow closure is tempting, but slower epithelialization is expected with aging and is not an infection cue on its own.
questions.takeaway: In older adults, watch for subtle infection cues (confusion, temperature above baseline, poor appetite) and protect fragile skin.

questions.stem: A client who had a skin lesion excised and sutured asks what happens in the wound during the first few days. Which statements by the nurse are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: “Macrophages arrive first, before any other white blood cells.”
“The blood vessels narrow at first to slow the bleeding.”
“Platelets clump together, and a fibrin clot seals the wound.”
“The dried clot on the surface forms a scab that acts like a bandage.”
“Some redness, swelling, and drainage in these first days is normal.”
“Collagen builds the wound's full strength within the first 3 days.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Neutrophils arrive first; macrophages follow.
Correct. Hemostasis begins with vasoconstriction of the injured vessels.
Correct. Platelets aggregate and a fibrin clot forms during hemostasis.
Correct. On the surface, the dried clot becomes a scab, a natural bandage.
Correct. Redness, edema, and exudate are normal early signs of the inflammatory phase.
Incorrect. Collagen is made during the proliferative phase (about day 3–21), and strength keeps building for months.
questions.rationale: The inflammatory phase starts at injury and lasts about 3–6 days. First comes hemostasis: injured vessels constrict, platelets clump, a fibrin clot forms, and the dried surface clot becomes a scab. Then nearby vessels widen and leak so white blood cells can enter, with neutrophils arriving first and macrophages following, which causes normal redness, edema, and exudate. The collagen statement is tempting because collagen is central to healing, but it belongs to the proliferative phase and does not reach full strength in days.
questions.takeaway: Inflammatory phase: vasoconstriction, clot and scab, then neutrophils before macrophages; redness, swelling, and drainage are normal.
questions.hintContent: Walk through the order: clot, clean, build. Which statements belong only to the first step?

questions.stem: The nurse reviews wound findings for several clients. Which findings are expected for the client's stage of healing? Select all that apply.
options: POD 1 after a sutured incision: mild redness and swelling along the suture line
POD 7 after a sutured incision: a firm ridge palpable beneath the incision
POD 5 after a sutured incision: spreading redness, increasing pain, and thick yellow drainage
Day 14 of an open wound: beefy red, bumpy tissue that bleeds slightly
POD 9 after a sutured incision in a client with obesity: no palpable ridge
Day 21 of an open wound: pale, dry tissue at the base
optionRationales: Correct. Mild redness and edema are normal inflammatory-phase findings on POD 1.
Correct. A healing ridge from new collagen is usually palpable by about the end of the first week.
Incorrect. Worsening redness and pain with purulent drainage around POD 4–5 suggest infection.
Correct. This is healthy proliferative-phase granulation.
Incorrect. No ridge by about POD 9 means inadequate collagen and a higher risk of dehiscence.
Incorrect. Pale, dry tissue suggests poor blood supply and poor healing.
questions.rationale: Healing follows a predictable timeline, so the same finding can be normal or abnormal depending on the day. Mild redness and swelling are expected early, a healing ridge is expected by about the end of the first week, and beefy red granulation that bleeds slightly is expected in an open wound in the proliferative phase. Spreading redness with purulent drainage on POD 5, no ridge by POD 9, and pale, dry granulation all break the expected pattern. The POD 9 finding is the easiest to miss because the incision may look closed, but the missing ridge shows weak collagen.
questions.takeaway: Ask “Is this what I should see on this day?” Early mild redness, a ridge by week 1, and beefy red granulation are expected.
questions.hintContent: Match each finding to the phase and day listed with it.
questions.hintStrategy: For multi-client SATA, evaluate each option against its own timeline; don't let one alarming option color the others.

questions.stem: A client with a newly sutured abdominal incision asks how long healing will take. Which statements should the nurse include in the teaching? Select all that apply.
options: “By 6 weeks, the scar will be back to the full strength of normal skin.”
“For the first several days, some redness and swelling are part of normal healing.”
“From about day 3 to day 21, new collagen builds strength in the incision.”
“By the end of the first week, you may feel a firm ridge under the incision.”
“The scar will keep changing and fading for 1 to 2 years.”
“Thick, yellow drainage around day 4 is a normal part of healing.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. A scar never regains the full strength of the original tissue.
Correct. The inflammatory phase lasts about 3–6 days, with expected redness, edema, and exudate.
Correct. The proliferative phase runs from about day 3 to day 21 as fibroblasts make collagen.
Correct. A healing ridge is usually palpable by about the end of the first week.
Correct. The maturation phase lasts from about day 21 to 1–2 years.
Incorrect. Thick, yellow (purulent) drainage suggests infection and should be reported.
questions.rationale: Teaching the normal timeline helps clients recognize problems early. The inflammatory phase (about 3–6 days) brings expected redness, swelling, and drainage; the proliferative phase (about day 3–21) builds collagen, and a healing ridge is usually felt by about the end of the first week; maturation lasts from about day 21 to 1–2 years as the scar flattens and fades. A scar never reaches the full strength of the original tissue, and purulent drainage is never a normal part of healing. The 6-week statement is tempting because the incision may look healed by then, but strength keeps building and never fully returns.
questions.takeaway: Inflammatory ≈3–6 days, proliferative ≈day 3–21, maturation ≈day 21 to 1–2 years; scars never regain full strength.
questions.hintContent: Line up each statement with the three phases and their usual timing.
questions.hintStrategy: In teaching SATA, eliminate any statement with an absolute claim (“full strength”) or one that normalizes a warning sign.

questions.stem: After an emergency bowel repair, a client's contaminated abdominal wound was left open with packing. The surgeon plans to close it once the swelling and contamination resolve. Which statements about this wound are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: “The wound is expected to be closed after about 3 to 5 days.”
“It was left open so swelling, drainage, or infection can resolve first.”
“It will likely scar more than a wound that was closed right away.”
“It will fill in from the bottom and never need to be closed.”
“Its infection risk is lower than that of a clean sutured incision.”
optionRationales: Correct. In tertiary intention, the wound is usually left open for about 3–5 days and then closed.
Correct. Edema, infection, or drainage are the reasons a wound is left open before delayed closure.
Correct. Because it was open first, tertiary intention leaves greater scarring than primary intention.
Incorrect. That describes secondary intention; this wound is planned for delayed closure.
Incorrect. A wound that was contaminated and left open has a higher infection risk than a clean primary closure.
questions.rationale: Tertiary intention, also called delayed primary closure, describes a wound that is left open for about 3–5 days because of edema, infection, or drainage, and then closed once it is clean. Because it sat open first, it scars more than a wound closed by primary intention, and its infection risk is moderate rather than low. A handy phrase is “open first, closed later = tertiary.” The “fill in from the bottom” statement is tempting because the wound is currently open and packed, but the surgeon plans to close it, which rules out secondary intention.
questions.takeaway: Tertiary intention: open about 3–5 days for swelling, infection, or drainage, then closed, with more scarring than primary.
questions.hintContent: Focus on the surgeon's plan to close the wound later; that detail sets the type of intention.
questions.hintStrategy: For SATA about one wound type, test each statement against that type's definition and eliminate features of the other types.

questions.stem: A client had an open abdominal hysterectomy. The nurse reviews the dressing documentation: 2 hours after surgery, a small amount of bright red drainage; POD 1, a small amount of pale pink, watery drainage; today (POD 2), a scant amount of clear, straw-colored drainage. Vital signs are stable. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Notify the surgeon that the drainage has changed color
Obtain a culture of the clear drainage at the next change
Document the expected progression and continue to monitor
Reinforce the dressing with extra gauze to absorb the drainage
optionRationales: Incorrect. Reporting a change in drainage is sometimes needed, but this change is toward lighter color and smaller amount, the expected healing pattern, so no report is needed.
Incorrect. Cultures are useful when drainage looks infected, but clear, scant drainage with stable vital signs shows no sign of infection.
Correct. Drainage that fades from sanguineous to serosanguineous to serous and decreases in amount is the expected postoperative pattern.
Incorrect. Reinforcing a dressing is appropriate for heavy drainage, but this drainage is scant, so extra gauze adds nothing; documenting and monitoring is what is needed.
questions.rationale: After surgery, incision drainage should follow a predictable pattern: sanguineous (bloody) right after surgery, serosanguineous (pale pink and watery) over the first day or two, then serous (clear), with the amount decreasing. This client's drainage is fading in color and shrinking in amount, so the nurse documents the expected progression and continues to monitor. Notifying the surgeon is tempting because the drainage changed, but a change toward clear and less is the healing direction. Drainage that goes back to bright red or turns purulent would need reporting.
questions.takeaway: Expected postoperative drainage fades from red to pink to clear and decreases in amount.
questions.hintContent: Look at the direction of the change in color and amount over time.
questions.hintStrategy: In trend questions, decide whether the change is moving toward normal or away from it before choosing to escalate.

questions.stem: A client with a slow-healing foot wound who was taught about the effects of smoking is found smoking outside the hospital entrance. The client says, “I know, I know. I've tried to quit before, and I just can't.” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “I know quitting is hard. Smoking narrows the blood vessels that feed your wound.”
“Quitting is hard. Would you like me to ask your provider about quit-smoking aids?”
“Switching to e-cigarettes would be a much safer way to protect your wound.”
“Even a few cigarettes a day slow healing, so cutting back is not enough.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Acknowledging the struggle and linking smoking to the wound are both helpful, but the client already knows the risk and needs concrete help to quit, which this response does not offer.
Correct. This response acknowledges the difficulty without judgment and offers concrete help, such as discussing nicotine replacement and a quit-smoking program with the provider.
Incorrect. Harm reduction is a reasonable idea, but e-cigarettes still deliver nicotine, which narrows the vessels that feed the wound, so this is not a safe substitute.
Incorrect. It is true that even a few cigarettes impair healing, but this response lectures and discourages a step toward quitting instead of offering help.
questions.rationale: Smoking slows healing in two ways: nicotine constricts blood vessels, and carbon monoxide takes oxygen's place on hemoglobin, so the wound is starved of oxygen. Because quitting is hard, the nurse responds without judgment, acknowledges the struggle, and offers concrete help, such as asking the provider about nicotine replacement options and a quit-smoking program. Any step toward quitting should be praised. The e-cigarette option is tempting because it sounds like harm reduction, but vaping still delivers nicotine and still narrows the vessels feeding the wound.
questions.takeaway: Respond to smoking without judgment and offer help to quit; vaping is not a safe swap for a healing wound.
questions.hintContent: Recall why nicotine, from any source, slows healing, and what support the nurse can offer.
questions.hintStrategy: For therapeutic responses, choose the option that acknowledges feelings and offers a realistic next step; eliminate judgment and inaccurate advice.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old client with an open sacral wound has eaten 30–40% of each meal for the past week and has lost 3 kg (6.6 lb) over the past month. Serum albumin is 2.8 g/dL. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Offer the client high-protein snacks between meals
Recheck the albumin in 1 month before changing the plan
Start a 3-day calorie count to measure the intake
Report the findings and request a nutrition consult
optionRationales: Incorrect. Protein snacks are a helpful nursing measure, but with weight loss, poor intake, and low albumin, the client needs a full nutrition plan from a dietitian, so this alone is incomplete.
Incorrect. Following lab trends is reasonable, but the data already show malnutrition, and waiting a month lets the wound stall.
Incorrect. A calorie count is a valid assessment tool, but intake, weight loss, and albumin already confirm the problem, so more data delays the needed referral.
Correct. Poor intake, unplanned weight loss, and albumin below about 3.5 g/dL point to malnutrition that will delay healing, so the nurse reports and requests a nutrition consult.
questions.rationale: Wound healing needs protein, calories, vitamins, and minerals, and malnutrition is one of the most common reasons a wound stalls. The cues here are classic: eating 50% or less of meals, unplanned weight loss, and an albumin of 2.8 g/dL, below about 3.5 g/dL. The nurse reports these findings and requests a nutrition consult so a dietitian can plan protein- and calorie-rich intake. Waiting to recheck the albumin is tempting because it seems cautious, but the problem is already clear and delay harms healing.
questions.takeaway: Eating ≤50% of meals, unplanned weight loss, and low albumin signal malnutrition; report and request a nutrition consult.
questions.hintContent: Count how many signs of poor nutrition the stem gives and what they mean for the wound.
questions.hintStrategy: When the data already confirm a problem, pick the action that addresses it now rather than one that delays.

questions.stem: The spouse of a client with an open abdominal wound that drains a moderate amount of serous fluid has been limiting the client's drinks, saying, “Less water in means less drainage out.” The client has no heart or kidney disease and no prescribed fluid restriction. Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Drinking enough keeps blood flowing to the wound, so please don't limit fluids.”
“Offer drinks freely, and I'll change the dressing as often as needed.”
“Ask the surgeon how much fluid is right for her before you give her more.”
“Some drainage is expected, so we'll measure the amount at each dressing change.”
optionRationales: Correct. Adequate fluids maintain blood flow and tissue hydration, which healing needs, unless a provider orders a restriction.
Incorrect. Offering fluids freely is the right action, but this response does not explain why fluids help healing, so the spouse may go back to limiting them.
Incorrect. Checking with the surgeon is reasonable when a restriction might be needed, but this client has no restriction or heart or kidney disease, so the nurse can teach now.
Incorrect. Monitoring drainage is a true and useful step, but it does not correct the spouse's belief that limiting fluids helps the wound.
questions.rationale: Healing depends on blood flow that brings oxygen, nutrients, and white blood cells to the wound. Adequate fluid intake keeps blood volume up and tissues hydrated, so a healing client should drink enough unless a provider orders a restriction for a condition such as heart or kidney disease. Limiting fluids does not dry up a wound in a helpful way, and it can actually slow healing. Simply offering drinks or measuring drainage is tempting, but the spouse needs to hear why fluids matter so the restriction stops.
questions.takeaway: Unless restricted, a healing client needs adequate fluids; limiting fluids does not help a wound.
questions.hintContent: Think about how blood flow and hydration relate to bringing supplies to the wound.
questions.hintStrategy: For family-teaching items, gently correct the misconception with the reason behind the correct practice.

questions.stem: During a preoperative phone call 1 week before an elective open abdominal surgery, a client mentions taking a full-strength aspirin every day “for heart health,” on the client's own. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Tell the client to stop taking the aspirin a week before surgery
Teach the client that aspirin increases bleeding risk
Notify the surgeon of the daily aspirin use before the surgery
Document the daily aspirin use in the record and take no other action
optionRationales: Incorrect. The aspirin may well need to be stopped before surgery, but that decision belongs to the surgeon; the nurse reports rather than changing the medication.
Incorrect. This teaching is accurate, but it is incomplete, because the surgeon still does not know about the aspirin and cannot plan for it.
Correct. Aspirin affects clotting and the inflammatory response, so the surgeon needs to know and decide how to manage it before surgery.
Incorrect. Documenting the finding is necessary, but documenting alone leaves the surgeon unaware of a bleeding and healing risk before the operation.
questions.rationale: Aspirin impairs healing because it interferes with platelets (clotting) and with the inflammatory response that starts the healing process. A client taking daily aspirin before surgery is at risk for bleeding and slowed healing, so the surgeon must be told in time to decide how to manage it. The nurse reports rather than independently stopping or adjusting the medication. Documenting only is the tempting choice because it records the finding, but it leaves the surgeon unaware of a risk that should be addressed before the operation.
questions.takeaway: Daily aspirin interferes with clotting and inflammation; report it to the surgeon before surgery.
questions.hintContent: Recall how aspirin affects the first phase of healing.
questions.hintStrategy: When a medication finding affects a planned procedure, choose the action that communicates it to the prescriber in time.

questions.stem: A client on POD 2 after an open colon resection declines to walk in the hall, saying, “I should stay in bed so my incision can heal.” The client is cleared to ambulate. Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Your surgeon cleared you to walk, so your incision is strong enough now.”
“Walking boosts circulation, which brings oxygen and nutrients to your incision.”
“Hold a pillow against your incision while walking so it feels more secure.”
“You can skip walking today if you eat extra protein at lunch instead.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. It is true that the surgeon cleared walking, but this response does not explain how walking helps healing, and an incision on POD 2 still has little strength.
Correct. Exercise pumps blood through the tissues, delivering oxygen and nutrients to the wound and carrying waste away.
Incorrect. Splinting is a helpful comfort tip, but it does not correct the client's belief that staying in bed is better for the incision.
Incorrect. Protein does support healing, but it cannot replace the circulation that walking provides, and the client is cleared to ambulate.
questions.rationale: Exercise improves circulation, and better circulation means faster healing. Moving the body pumps blood through the tissues, bringing oxygen and nutrients to the wound and carrying waste away, so walking as allowed after surgery is a simple, powerful healing tool. The nurse corrects the client's belief with the reason walking helps the incision. Offering extra protein instead is tempting because nutrition matters, but it does not replace the blood flow that activity provides.
questions.takeaway: Walking as allowed improves circulation and speeds wound healing.
questions.hintContent: Think about what activity does for blood flow to the incision.
questions.hintStrategy: For a best-response item, choose the option that corrects the misconception with the accurate reason.

questions.stem: A client with a BMI of 34 has a Stage 3 pressure injury. The client says, “I'm going to cut down to 800 calories a day so I can lose weight while this heals.” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Losing weight will help your wound heal, so a slower weight loss would be safer.”
“Be sure to take a daily multivitamin with extra vitamin C while you cut calories.”
“Cut out carbohydrates and fats completely, but keep your protein intake high.”
“Too few calories makes your body burn protein for energy instead of building tissue.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Obesity does delay healing, but this response still endorses dieting during healing, when the body needs extra calories and protein.
Incorrect. Vitamins support collagen formation, but they do not replace the energy the body needs, and this response accepts a severe calorie cut.
Incorrect. Keeping protein high sounds balanced, but without enough carbohydrates and fats, the body burns that protein for energy instead of building tissue.
Correct. When calories are too low, protein is used for fuel instead of collagen and new cells, so healing slows.
questions.rationale: Obesity does delay healing, but a severe calorie cut during healing makes things worse. Carbohydrates and fats supply energy; when calories are too low, the body burns protein for fuel instead of using it to build collagen and new cells, so the wound is starved of building material. The nurse explains this and can suggest discussing weight goals with the provider or a dietitian after the wound has healed. Cutting carbohydrates and fats while keeping protein high is tempting because it sounds balanced, but without enough energy the protein still gets burned for fuel.
questions.takeaway: A healing client should not cut calories; too few calories forces the body to burn protein instead of building tissue.
questions.hintContent: Recall what carbohydrates and fats do for protein during healing.
questions.hintStrategy: When both options seem to address a real risk (obesity), choose the one that protects healing right now.

questions.stem: Refer to the Laboratory Results for a 64-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes who is on POD 3 after an open bowel resection. Which finding should the nurse address first to promote wound healing?
options: Fasting glucose 312 mg/dL
Serum albumin 3.3 g/dL
White blood cells 9,800/mm³
Hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL
optionRationales: Correct. High glucose impairs white blood cell function and blood flow, raising infection risk and slowing healing; it needs treatment and reporting now.
Incorrect. Albumin is slightly low and should be addressed with nutrition, but it is not the most urgent finding.
Incorrect. This WBC count is within normal limits.
Incorrect. This hemoglobin is within the normal range for an adult female and is not the priority.
questions.rationale: Diabetes is one of the most important factors affecting healing. High glucose impairs white blood cell function, so the body cannot fight bacteria well, and long-term diabetes damages the vessels that bring blood and oxygen to the wound. A fasting glucose of 312 mg/dL is markedly elevated and should be treated per protocol and reported so treatment can be adjusted. The slightly low albumin is tempting because nutrition matters for healing, but it is a milder, slower-moving problem than the acutely high glucose.
questions.takeaway: Glucose control is wound care: high glucose impairs WBCs and blood flow and should be treated and reported first.
questions.hintContent: Find the most abnormal value and connect it to infection risk and healing.
questions.hintStrategy: With several lab values, address the one furthest from normal that most directly threatens the client right now.

questions.stem: On POD 1 after an open appendectomy, the nurse removes the dressing and finds a small amount of pale pink, watery drainage. How should the nurse document the drainage?
options: Sanguineous (hemorrhagic)
Serous
Serosanguineous
Purosanguineous
optionRationales: Incorrect. Sanguineous drainage is bright or dark red blood, not pale pink and watery.
Incorrect. Serous drainage is clear and straw-colored, with no blood tinge.
Correct. Pale pink, watery drainage is clear fluid tinged with blood, which is serosanguineous and common in new surgical incisions.
Incorrect. Purosanguineous drainage is thick pus mixed with blood, seen in infected wounds.
questions.rationale: Exudate names describe their ingredients: “sero” means serum (clear fluid), “sanguin” means blood, and “puru” means pus. Pale pink, watery drainage is clear fluid with a small amount of blood, so it is serosanguineous, an expected finding in a new surgical incision on POD 1. Sanguineous drainage is frankly red, serous is clear, and purosanguineous is thick and pus-filled. Serous is the tempting answer because the drainage is watery, but the pink tinge shows blood is present.
questions.takeaway: Pale pink and watery = serosanguineous, common and expected in new incisions.
questions.hintContent: Break the exudate names into their parts and match them to the color and thickness described.
questions.hintStrategy: For documentation items, match every descriptor in the stem (color and consistency) to the term, not just one.

questions.stem: A client with a Stage 3 pressure injury and no dietary restrictions asks the nurse for help choosing lunch from the hospital menu. Which meal best supports wound healing?
options: Spinach and strawberry salad with a glass of orange juice
Grilled salmon, black beans, and sliced bell peppers
Pasta with marinara sauce, garlic bread, and iced tea
Egg white omelet with white toast and coffee
optionRationales: Incorrect. This meal is rich in vitamin C, which helps make collagen, but it supplies very little protein, the main building block the wound needs.
Correct. Fish and beans provide protein and minerals, and bell peppers provide vitamin C for collagen formation.
Incorrect. Pasta and bread provide calories for energy, but this meal has little protein and few of the vitamins and minerals a healing wound needs.
Incorrect. Egg whites supply protein, but this meal lacks vitamin C and minerals such as zinc, so it is less complete than the salmon meal.
questions.rationale: A healing wound needs more protein, plus carbohydrates and fats for energy, vitamins A and C, iron, zinc, and copper. Protein is the raw material for collagen and new cells, and vitamin C is needed to make strong collagen. Salmon and black beans supply protein and minerals, and bell peppers supply vitamin C. The spinach salad is tempting because it seems healthy and has vitamin C, but it gives the wound almost no protein; the other meals each cover only part of what the wound needs.
questions.takeaway: Choose meals with protein plus vitamin C (and zinc and iron) to support wound healing.
questions.hintContent: Look for the meal that contains a protein source and a vitamin C source.
questions.hintStrategy: In diet-choice items, check each option for the specific nutrients the condition needs, not for how “light” or “healthy” it sounds.

questions.stem: A Muslim client with a healing leg wound plans to fast from dawn to sunset during Ramadan. The client asks, “Can I still fast while my wound heals?” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “You'll need to stop fasting completely until the wound has fully healed.”
“Many faiths excuse people who are ill from fasting; you could ask your imam.”
“Fasting is your choice; just be sure to drink plenty of water at night.”
“Let's plan protein-rich meals and medicine times for before dawn and after sunset.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Stopping the fast may seem safest for the wound, but it ignores the client's values and autonomy when a workable plan is possible.
Incorrect. Many faiths do exempt people who are ill, and involving a religious leader can help, but this response passes the decision away instead of planning care with the client.
Incorrect. Respecting the choice and encouraging fluids are good, but this response is incomplete, because it does not plan for the protein and medication timing the wound needs.
Correct. This respects the practice and collaborates on meal and medication timing that protects healing.
questions.rationale: Culturally competent care means asking about and respecting the client's beliefs, food customs, and practices before planning. When a practice such as fasting could affect healing, the nurse does not dismiss it; instead, the nurse discusses it respectfully and collaborates on adjustments, such as timing protein-rich meals and medications in the hours before dawn and after sunset. This protects healing while honoring the client's beliefs. Telling the client to stop fasting is tempting because it seems safest for the wound, but it ignores the client's values and autonomy.
questions.takeaway: When a cultural practice may affect healing, collaborate on adjustments rather than dismissing the practice.
questions.hintContent: Look for the response that supports both healing and the client's beliefs.
questions.hintStrategy: For cultural-care items, eliminate options that dismiss, override, or hand off the client's values; choose collaboration.

questions.stem: A client with a BMI of 43 is scheduled for an open abdominal surgery. The client says, “I eat plenty of food, so why would my weight slow down my healing?” Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Fatty tissue has a poor blood supply, and extra weight pulls on the incision.”
“Extra weight gives your body more stored protein, so healing is faster.”
“Weight matters for healing only if you also have diabetes.”
“Fatty tissue makes extra white blood cells, and those cells slow down healing.”
optionRationales: Correct. Adipose tissue has a poor blood supply, so less oxygen and fewer WBCs reach the wound, and extra weight puts tension on the suture line.
Incorrect. Obesity delays healing; stored fat does not supply protein for wound repair.
Incorrect. Obesity delays healing on its own, even without diabetes.
Incorrect. The problem is poor blood supply to fatty tissue, which means fewer WBCs and less oxygen reach the wound.
questions.rationale: Malnutrition and obesity both delay healing, but for different reasons. Fatty (adipose) tissue has a poor blood supply, so less oxygen and fewer white blood cells reach the wound, and extra weight puts tension on the suture line, raising the risk that the incision will pull apart. A person can also be obese and malnourished at the same time. The diabetes option is tempting because the two conditions often occur together, but obesity delays healing by itself.
questions.takeaway: Obesity delays healing through poor blood supply in fatty tissue and tension on the suture line.
questions.hintContent: Think about blood flow in adipose tissue and mechanical stress on the incision.
questions.hintStrategy: For “why” items, choose the option that names the mechanism; eliminate options that add a condition the stem doesn't require.

questions.stem: A client receiving cyclophosphamide for lymphoma has a 2-week-old surgical incision from a port placement that is healing slowly. The client asks why. Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Chemotherapy thins your blood, so the wound keeps oozing instead of closing.”
“Chemotherapy causes extra inflammation, which stops collagen from forming.”
“It kills fast-dividing cells, including new wound cells, and lowers your white cells.”
“Chemotherapy doesn't affect healing; the slow closure is from the port itself.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Interfering with platelets is how aspirin affects healing; it is not the main way chemotherapy slows healing.
Incorrect. Chemotherapy suppresses, rather than increases, the cells involved in healing.
Correct. Chemotherapy targets rapidly dividing cells, including the new cells a wound needs, and lowers WBCs, which slows healing and raises infection risk.
Incorrect. Chemotherapy is a known cause of impaired wound healing.
questions.rationale: Chemotherapy drugs such as cyclophosphamide work by killing rapidly dividing cells. Unfortunately, the new cells a wound needs to rebuild tissue also divide rapidly, and chemotherapy lowers white blood cell counts, so healing slows and infection risk rises. The nurse explains this and monitors the incision closely for subtle signs of infection. The “thins your blood” option is tempting because many clients link medications to bleeding, but that mechanism belongs to aspirin.
questions.takeaway: Chemotherapy impairs healing by killing rapidly dividing cells and lowering WBCs.
questions.hintContent: Recall how chemotherapy works against cancer cells and which healthy cells share that feature.
questions.hintStrategy: When options pair drugs with mechanisms, match each drug to its own mechanism; eliminate options that borrow another drug's effect.

questions.stem: A client whose infected toe wound has healed asks the nurse to request a prescription for antibiotics to take “every day from now on, just in case.” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “I'll ask your provider, since your toe infection could come back.”
“Long-term antibiotics can lead to resistant infections that are harder to treat.”
“Check your feet every day so a new infection is caught early.”
“Antibiotics only stop working if you skip some of the doses that you are prescribed.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Relaying requests to the provider is part of the nurse's role, but this response supports an unsafe plan without teaching about resistance.
Correct. Bacteria that survive repeated exposure become resistant, so future infections are harder to treat.
Incorrect. Daily foot checks are excellent prevention, but this response does not answer the request or explain why long-term antibiotics are a problem.
Incorrect. Skipping doses does promote resistance, but long-term use alone also breeds resistant bacteria, so this statement is misleading.
questions.rationale: Long-term antibiotic use carries the risk of resistant infections. When bacteria are exposed to antibiotics again and again, the ones that survive become resistant, so the next infection is harder to treat. The nurse explains this and redirects the client toward prevention, such as good wound care, nutrition, and glucose control. The missed-doses option is tempting because it is a familiar resistance message, but long-term use alone also breeds resistance.
questions.takeaway: Long-term antibiotics breed resistant infections; they are not a prevention plan.
questions.hintContent: Recall the specific risk of long-term antibiotic use.
questions.hintStrategy: For medication-teaching responses, choose the option with an accurate risk explanation; eliminate partial truths.

questions.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes whose glucose readings have been 250–280 mg/dL has a foot wound that is healing slowly. The client asks, “What does my blood sugar have to do with my foot?” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Extra sugar in your blood feeds the new tissue, so it helps healing.”
“Blood sugar only affects your eyes and kidneys, not the wound on your foot.”
“High sugar makes the wound bleed more, which washes away new tissue.”
“High sugar weakens white blood cells and damages the vessels that bring oxygen.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. High glucose impairs healing; it does not nourish new tissue.
Incorrect. High glucose directly affects white blood cells and blood flow to wounds.
Incorrect. Bleeding is not how high glucose affects healing.
Correct. High glucose impairs WBC function, and long-term diabetes damages blood vessels, reducing blood and oxygen to the wound.
questions.rationale: Diabetes slows healing in two ways. High blood glucose impairs white blood cell function, so the body cannot fight bacteria well, and long-term diabetes damages blood vessels, so less blood and oxygen reach the wound. That is why glucose control is wound care, and persistently high readings are reported so treatment can be adjusted. The option about sugar feeding new tissue is tempting because glucose is an energy source, but high blood levels hurt rather than help the healing process.
questions.takeaway: High glucose impairs WBC function and blood flow, so glucose control is wound care.
questions.hintContent: Think about what high glucose does to infection-fighting cells and to blood vessels.
questions.hintStrategy: For pathophysiology explanations, choose the option that names both mechanisms named in the condition, not a plausible-sounding guess.

questions.stem: A client is being discharged with a healing surgical wound. The discharge instructions list both aspirin and acetaminophen as acceptable for mild pain. The client asks, “Which one is better for my wound?” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Acetaminophen doesn't interfere with healing the way aspirin can.”
“Both affect healing the same way, so choose whichever you prefer.”
“Aspirin is better because it reduces the inflammation that slows healing.”
“Neither is safe, because all pain relievers slow wound healing.”
optionRationales: Correct. Aspirin interferes with platelets and the inflammatory response; acetaminophen relieves pain without those effects.
Incorrect. Aspirin impairs healing, while acetaminophen is not listed as impairing it.
Incorrect. Inflammation is a needed phase of healing, and aspirin interferes with it and with platelets.
Incorrect. Acetaminophen is not listed as impairing healing, and pain control supports recovery.
questions.rationale: Aspirin impairs healing because it interferes with platelets (clotting) and with the inflammatory response the wound needs to start healing. Acetaminophen relieves pain without those anti-inflammatory or anti-platelet effects, so it is not listed as impairing healing. When both are allowed, acetaminophen is the better choice for the wound. The aspirin option is tempting because “less inflammation” sounds good, but inflammation is the step that cleans the wound and signals rebuilding.
questions.takeaway: Aspirin impairs healing (platelets and inflammation); acetaminophen does not.
questions.hintContent: Remember that inflammation is a needed phase of healing, not just a symptom.
questions.hintStrategy: When a choice claims a drug helps by blocking a normal process, check whether that process is needed.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews drainage documentation written by a nursing student for several clients. Which entries correctly match the description with the exudate type? Select all that apply.
options: Clear, straw-colored fluid from an intact blister: purulent
Pale pink, watery drainage from a POD 1 incision: serosanguineous
Thick, cream-colored drainage streaked with red: purosanguineous
Bright red drainage on a dressing 1 hour after surgery: sanguineous
Thick, opaque, green drainage with a foul odor: serosanguineous
optionRationales: Incorrect. Clear, straw-colored fluid is serous; purulent drainage is thick, opaque pus.
Correct. Clear fluid tinged with blood that is pale pink and watery is serosanguineous.
Correct. Pus mixed with blood is purosanguineous, seen in infected wounds.
Correct. Bright or dark red, bloody drainage is sanguineous.
Incorrect. Thick, opaque, colored, foul-smelling drainage is purulent.
questions.rationale: Each exudate name describes its contents: serous is clear, watery, and straw-colored; sanguineous is bright or dark red blood; serosanguineous is clear fluid tinged pink with blood; purulent is thick, opaque pus that may be yellow, green, or blue; and purosanguineous is pus mixed with blood. Matching each description to these definitions shows three correct entries. The blister entry is tempting to accept because blister fluid is a classic example, but it is the classic example of serous, not purulent, drainage.
questions.takeaway: Serous = clear; sanguineous = red; serosanguineous = pink and watery; purulent = thick pus; purosanguineous = pus plus blood.
questions.hintContent: Translate each term into its parts (serum, blood, pus) and compare with the description.
questions.hintStrategy: In matching SATA, check both halves of each pair; a correct description paired with the wrong term is incorrect.

questions.stem: A Hindu client who follows a lacto-vegetarian diet (dairy, but no meat, fish, or eggs) has a pressure injury. Which foods could the nurse suggest to increase protein, vitamin C, or zinc while respecting the client's beliefs? Select all that apply.
options: Lentil dal
Grilled chicken
Plain yogurt
Chickpea curry
Hard-boiled eggs
Oranges and bell peppers
optionRationales: Correct. Lentils provide protein and minerals and fit a lacto-vegetarian diet.
Incorrect. Chicken is meat, which conflicts with the client's diet.
Correct. Dairy is allowed in a lacto-vegetarian diet and provides protein.
Correct. Chickpeas (a type of bean) provide protein and zinc and fit the client's diet.
Incorrect. Eggs are excluded from a lacto-vegetarian diet.
Correct. These are good sources of vitamin C, which is needed for collagen.
questions.rationale: Culturally competent nutrition teaching starts with what the client already eats and believes. A lacto-vegetarian diet includes dairy but excludes meat, fish, and eggs, so protein can come from lentils, beans such as chickpeas, and dairy foods such as yogurt, while fruits and vegetables such as oranges and bell peppers add vitamin C. Suggesting chicken or eggs ignores the client's beliefs, even though both are good protein sources. Eggs are the most tempting distractor because many vegetarians eat them, but this client's diet excludes them.
questions.takeaway: Fit healing nutrients (protein, vitamin C, zinc) into the client's own food practices.
questions.hintContent: Check every food against both the nutrients needed and the client's stated diet.
questions.hintStrategy: In cultural-nutrition SATA, an option must meet both conditions in the stem: the nutrient need and the client's beliefs.

questions.stem: After teaching a client who smokes about how smoking affects healing of a leg wound, the nurse evaluates the client's understanding. Which statements by the client indicate that the teaching was effective? Select all that apply.
options: “Vaping won't affect my wound because there's no smoke.”
“Nicotine narrows my blood vessels, so less blood gets to my wound.”
“Carbon monoxide in smoke takes the place of oxygen in my blood.”
“I'll ask my provider about nicotine replacement and a quit program.”
“Smoking only hurts my lungs, so my leg wound won't be affected.”
“If I smoke only after meals, it won't affect my healing.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Vaping still delivers nicotine, which still constricts blood vessels.
Correct. Nicotine causes vasoconstriction, reducing blood flow to the wound.
Correct. Carbon monoxide binds to hemoglobin in place of oxygen, so each red blood cell carries less oxygen.
Correct. Seeking support to quit is an appropriate step the nurse encourages.
Incorrect. Smoking reduces oxygen delivery to all tissues, including wounds.
Incorrect. Any smoking delivers nicotine and carbon monoxide, which impair healing.
questions.rationale: Smoking starves a wound of oxygen in two ways: nicotine constricts blood vessels so less blood reaches the wound, and carbon monoxide binds to hemoglobin in place of oxygen so each red blood cell carries less oxygen. Statements that describe these effects, or a plan to seek help quitting, show the teaching worked. Vaping is the common trap: it removes the smoke but not the nicotine, so blood vessels still constrict. Limiting when the client smokes does not remove either harmful effect.
questions.takeaway: Smoking cuts wound oxygen through nicotine vasoconstriction and carbon monoxide; vaping still delivers nicotine.
questions.hintContent: Recall the two ways smoking reduces oxygen delivery and whether vaping removes either one.
questions.hintStrategy: In evaluation SATA, select statements that are accurate and show a safe plan; reject partial measures presented as solutions.

questions.stem: The nurse has taught a client with an open surgical wound about nutrition for healing. Which statements by the client show correct understanding? Select all that apply.
options: “I need protein because it's the raw material for new tissue and collagen.”
“Vitamin C helps my body make strong collagen.”
“I should cut out carbohydrates so my body uses protein for energy.”
“Iron helps my blood carry oxygen to the wound.”
“Zinc helps my body build collagen and new cells.”
“Vitamin A is needed only for my eyes, not for my skin.”
optionRationales: Correct. Protein supplies the building blocks for collagen, new cells, and immune cells.
Correct. Vitamin C is needed to make strong collagen and supports immune function.
Incorrect. Carbohydrates and fats supply energy so that protein is spared for building tissue.
Correct. Iron builds hemoglobin, which carries oxygen to the wound.
Correct. Zinc and copper are minerals used to build collagen and make new cells.
Incorrect. Vitamin A supports epithelial (skin surface) growth and the inflammatory response.
questions.rationale: New tissue is built from what the client eats. Protein is the raw material for collagen and new cells, vitamin C helps make strong collagen, vitamin A supports epithelial growth, iron builds hemoglobin to carry oxygen, and zinc and copper help build collagen and new cells. Carbohydrates and fats supply energy so the body does not burn protein for fuel. The carbohydrate statement is tempting because it sounds like a protein-first plan, but cutting carbohydrates causes protein to be burned for energy instead of building tissue.
questions.takeaway: Healing needs protein, energy from carbohydrates and fats, vitamins A and C, iron, zinc, and copper.
questions.hintContent: Match each nutrient with its job in building and feeding new tissue.
questions.hintStrategy: In client-statement SATA, check each statement for an accurate role; watch for statements that sound health-conscious but undermine healing.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews incision drainage findings for several postoperative clients. Which findings should the nurse report to the provider? Select all that apply.
options: POD 1: a small amount of pale pink, watery drainage
POD 4: thick, yellow-green, foul-smelling drainage
POD 2: drainage that had become pink and watery is now bright red and increasing, with a rising heart rate
POD 3: a scant amount of clear, straw-colored drainage
POD 5: thick, cream-colored drainage streaked with blood and a temperature of 38.3 °C (100.9 °F)
One hour after surgery: a small amount of bright red drainage on the dressing
optionRationales: Incorrect. Small serosanguineous drainage on POD 1 is expected.
Correct. Thick, colored, foul-smelling drainage is purulent and indicates infection.
Correct. Drainage going backward to bright red with a rising heart rate suggests new bleeding.
Incorrect. Scant serous drainage by POD 3 follows the expected pattern.
Correct. Purosanguineous drainage with fever indicates infection.
Incorrect. A small amount of sanguineous drainage right after surgery is expected.
questions.rationale: Normal incision drainage fades from sanguineous to serosanguineous to serous and decreases in amount. Two changes break that pattern and need reporting: drainage that goes backward to bright red, especially with a rising heart rate (possible hemorrhage), and drainage that turns purulent or purosanguineous, often around POD 4–5 with fever (infection). The small amount of bright red drainage 1 hour after surgery is the tempting distractor, but sanguineous drainage right after surgery is expected; it is the return of red after the drainage has lightened that is concerning.
questions.takeaway: Report drainage that returns to bright red or turns purulent or purosanguineous; fading color and amount is expected.
questions.hintContent: For each finding, compare the drainage with what is expected on that postoperative day.
questions.hintStrategy: When the same color appears in several options, use the timing and trend to decide which one is abnormal.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old client in a skilled nursing facility has a Stage 3 pressure injury. Which findings indicate malnutrition that may delay healing? Select all that apply.
options: Serum albumin of 2.9 g/dL
Eats about 40% of each meal
Weight stable over the past 6 months
Lost 5 kg (11 lb) in 2 months without trying
Serum albumin of 4.1 g/dL last month
optionRationales: Correct. Albumin below about 3.5 g/dL can signal poor protein status and poor healing.
Correct. Eating 50% or less of meals is a cue of malnutrition.
Incorrect. Stable weight does not suggest malnutrition.
Correct. Unplanned weight loss is a key sign of malnutrition.
Incorrect. An albumin of 4.1 g/dL is within the normal range.
questions.rationale: Malnutrition means the body is missing the building blocks for new tissue. Key cues include unplanned weight loss, eating 50% or less of meals, and a low albumin (below about 3.5 g/dL, such as 2.9 g/dL). When these appear in a client with a wound, the nurse reports them and requests a nutrition consult as appropriate. The older normal albumin is the tempting distractor, but last month's value does not cancel the current low result, poor intake, and weight loss.
questions.takeaway: Unplanned weight loss, eating ≤50% of meals, and albumin below about 3.5 g/dL signal malnutrition.
questions.hintContent: Compare each value with the cutoffs for poor intake and low albumin.
questions.hintStrategy: In assessment SATA, use the most current data and known cutoffs to decide each option.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old client with type 2 diabetes who smokes is being discharged with a healing foot wound. The client has no prescribed fluid restriction. Which instructions should the nurse include to promote healing? Select all that apply.
options: “Switch to e-cigarettes, which won't affect your wound.”
“Walk as your provider allows to improve circulation to your foot.”
“Include a protein food such as eggs, fish, or beans at every meal.”
“Check your blood glucose as prescribed and report readings that stay high.”
“Drink less water so the wound produces less drainage.”
“Talk with your provider about nicotine replacement and a quit program.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Vaping still delivers nicotine, which constricts blood vessels.
Correct. Exercise improves circulation, bringing oxygen and nutrients to the wound.
Correct. Protein is the raw material for collagen and new tissue.
Correct. High glucose impairs WBC function and blood flow, so glucose control is wound care.
Incorrect. Without a prescribed restriction, adequate fluids support blood flow and healing.
Correct. Support to quit smoking addresses a major factor that slows healing.
questions.rationale: Much of what helps healing is in the client's hands, so health-promotion teaching is powerful wound care. Walking improves circulation, protein supplies building material, glucose control protects white blood cell function and blood flow, and quitting smoking restores oxygen delivery. Vaping and limiting fluids both sound like reasonable compromises, but vaping still delivers nicotine and limiting fluids reduces the blood flow the wound needs. The e-cigarette instruction is the most tempting trap because clients often see it as a safe swap.
questions.takeaway: Promote healing with activity, protein, glucose control, and quitting nicotine, not vaping or fluid limits.
questions.hintContent: Match each instruction to a factor that helps or hurts healing for this client.
questions.hintStrategy: In health-promotion SATA, include instructions that address each risk factor in the stem; reject “compromises” that keep the harmful factor.

questions.stem: Refer to the client's Health History and Medication List. The client is a 66-year-old with a slow-healing surgical wound. Which findings are factors likely to be delaying this client's healing? Select all that apply.

rows: 650 mg orally every 6 hours as needed

options: BMI of 38
Prednisone 10 mg daily
Walks 20 minutes twice daily
Aspirin 325 mg daily
Acetaminophen 650 mg as needed
Vitamin C 500 mg daily
optionRationales: Correct. Obesity delays healing because fatty tissue has a poor blood supply and extra weight stresses the suture line.
Correct. Steroids suppress the inflammation the wound needs, slow collagen formation, and raise infection risk.
Incorrect. Walking improves circulation and supports healing.
Correct. Aspirin interferes with platelets and with the inflammatory response.
Incorrect. Acetaminophen is not listed as impairing wound healing.
Incorrect. Vitamin C supports collagen formation and healing.
questions.rationale: When looking for reasons a wound is healing slowly, the nurse sorts the data into factors that hurt and factors that help. Obesity, long-term steroids, and aspirin all impair healing: fatty tissue has a poor blood supply, steroids suppress inflammation and collagen formation, and aspirin interferes with platelets and inflammation. Walking, vitamin C, and acetaminophen do not delay healing, and the first two support it. Acetaminophen is the tempting distractor because it is a pain reliever like aspirin, but it lacks aspirin's anti-platelet and anti-inflammatory effects.
questions.takeaway: Obesity, steroids, aspirin, and chemotherapy delay healing; activity and vitamin C support it; acetaminophen is not listed as impairing it.

questions.stem: An unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP) tells the RN that a client on POD 6 after an open bowel resection just vomited and then said, “I felt something pop in my belly.” Which action should the RN take first?
options: Call the surgeon to report a possible wound dehiscence
Give the prescribed antiemetic and then check the incision
Go to the bedside and inspect the incision now
Ask the UAP to look under the dressing and report back
optionRationales: Incorrect. The RN needs assessment data before calling, and going to the bedside takes only moments.
Incorrect. Treating nausea first delays assessment of a possible dehiscence that could progress to evisceration.
Correct. A “pop” after vomiting is a classic cue of dehiscence; the RN assesses the incision immediately.
Incorrect. Assessing a possible complication requires RN judgment and cannot be delegated.
questions.rationale: A client who feels something “pop” after coughing, sneezing, or vomiting near the end of the first week is describing a classic sign of dehiscence. The RN goes to the bedside right away to inspect the incision, because dehiscence is urgent and can progress to evisceration. If the edges have separated, the nurse stays, positions the client in low Fowler's with knees bent, covers the wound with sterile saline-moistened dressings, and notifies the surgeon. Calling the surgeon first is tempting, but the RN needs to assess before reporting, and the bedside is seconds away.
questions.takeaway: “I felt something pop” after a cough, sneeze, or vomiting means: go assess the incision now.
questions.hintContent: Recall what a “popping” sensation near the end of the first week suggests.
questions.hintStrategy: Assess before you act or call, unless the stem already gives the assessment data; assessment is never delegated to UAP.

questions.stem: Three hours after open reduction and internal fixation of a femur fracture, a client becomes restless and anxious. The heart rate has risen from 82 to 104/min, and blood pressure is 126/78 mm Hg, unchanged from baseline. The dressing is dry. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Give the prescribed as-needed anxiolytic to calm the client
Assess the thigh for swelling and check vital signs and urine output
Reassure the client that this is common and recheck the vital signs again in 1 hour
Coach the client in slow, deep breathing to ease the anxiety
optionRationales: Incorrect. Treating restlessness with a sedative could mask an early sign of bleeding.
Correct. Restlessness and tachycardia can be early signs of concealed bleeding; a dry dressing does not rule it out.
Incorrect. Restlessness with a rising heart rate early after surgery needs assessment now, not in an hour.
Incorrect. Coaching breathing treats a symptom without assessing for a possible hemorrhage.
questions.rationale: Hemorrhage risk is greatest in the first 48 hours after surgery, and bleeding can be internal while the dressing stays dry. Restlessness and anxiety are often the earliest signs of blood loss because the brain senses less oxygen, and the heart rate climbs to compensate; a falling blood pressure is a later sign. The nurse assesses the surgical site for swelling or a hematoma and checks vital signs and urine output before treating the anxiety. The anxiolytic is tempting because the client appears anxious, but sedating the client could hide the earliest warning of bleeding.
questions.takeaway: Early postoperative restlessness with a rising heart rate is a bleeding cue until proven otherwise, even with a dry dressing and normal BP.
questions.hintContent: Think about which signs of blood loss appear early and which appear late.
questions.hintStrategy: When a new symptom could be physical or emotional, assess for the physical cause before treating it as anxiety.

questions.stem: Two hours after excision of a large lipoma from the upper back, a client's dressing is saturated with bright red blood that is now trickling onto the sheets. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Remove the dressing to find the bleeding source
Call the surgeon to report active bleeding
Check the most recent hemoglobin result
Apply firm, direct pressure over the dressing
optionRationales: Incorrect. Removing the dressing can disrupt clots and increase bleeding; pressure is applied over it and reinforced.
Incorrect. The surgeon must be notified, but controlling active bleeding with pressure comes first.
Incorrect. Reviewing labs does not stop the bleeding that is happening now.
Correct. For external bleeding, direct pressure is the immediate action to slow blood loss while help is summoned.
questions.rationale: Hemorrhage is most likely in the first 48 hours, when clots are new and fragile, and it can come from a slipped stitch or a dislodged clot. When bleeding is external and active, the first action is to apply direct pressure and reinforce the dressing to slow blood loss. Then the nurse stays with the client, has the surgeon notified promptly, and monitors vital signs, urine output, and hemoglobin. Calling the surgeon is the tempting answer because the client may need to return to surgery, but pressure controls the immediate threat.
questions.takeaway: Active external bleeding: apply direct pressure and reinforce first, then notify the surgeon.
questions.hintContent: Ask which action directly slows the blood loss happening right now.
questions.hintStrategy: When a client is actively losing blood, choose the hands-on action that stops the loss before calls, labs, or documentation.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes and Vital Signs for a client with an evisceration. Which action should the nurse take next?

rows: Called to room after client coughed. Loops of bowel protruding through midline incision. Stayed with client; charge nurse called surgeon.
Bowel covered with sterile dressings moistened with sterile normal saline. Low Fowler's position with knees flexed.
Client restless, saying “Something is wrong.” Skin cool and clammy.

options: Report the signs of shock to the surgeon and prepare for emergency surgery
Remoisten the dressings with sterile normal saline
Raise the head of the bed to high Fowler's position to ease the client's breathing
Recheck the blood pressure in 15 minutes to confirm the trend
optionRationales: Correct. Rising heart rate, falling blood pressure, restlessness, and cool, clammy skin are signs of shock that must be reported while the client is prepared for surgery.
Incorrect. Keeping the dressings moist protects the bowel and is ongoing care, but the client is now showing shock, which is the more urgent problem.
Incorrect. Easing breathing seems helpful, but high Fowler's increases abdominal pressure and tension on the open wound; low Fowler's with knees bent is maintained.
Incorrect. Trending vital signs is reasonable, but three readings already show shock developing, and waiting delays emergency surgery.
questions.rationale: Evisceration is a surgical emergency in which organs protrude through an opened incision. After the nurse stays with the client, covers the organs with sterile saline-moistened dressings, positions the client in low Fowler's with knees bent, and notifies the surgeon, the next priority is monitoring for shock. This client's trend (heart rate climbing to 128/min, blood pressure falling to 90/56 mm Hg, restlessness, cool clammy skin) shows shock developing, so the nurse reports it right away and prepares the client for surgery while keeping the client NPO. Rechecking the blood pressure is tempting because it seems careful, but the trend is already clear and waiting delays surgery.
questions.takeaway: After evisceration care is started, watch for shock (tachycardia, falling BP, restlessness, cool clammy skin) and prepare for surgery, keeping the client NPO.
questions.hintContent: Read the vital sign trend and decide what it means for a client with exposed organs.

Temp 38.2 °C (100.8 °F); redness spreading 1 cm past incision; scant thick yellow drainage
Pain 5/10; small amount of serosanguineous drainage
Incision itchy; firm ridge palpable; afebrile

options: Client 3: POD 1 after knee arthroplasty
Client 2: POD 4 after bowel resection
Client 1: POD 7 after midline laparotomy
Client 4: POD 10 after cesarean birth
optionRationales: Incorrect. Moderate pain and a small amount of serosanguineous drainage on POD 1 are expected.
Incorrect. Fever with spreading redness suggests infection, which needs attention but is less immediately dangerous than a possible dehiscence.
Correct. A “pop” after sneezing with a large gush of salmon-colored drainage suggests dehiscence, which is urgent and can progress to evisceration.
Incorrect. An itchy incision with a palpable ridge is an expected finding of healing.

Client 1 felt a “pop” after sneezing and has a large gush of salmon-colored drainage, the classic picture of dehiscence, which can progress to evisceration, a surgical emergency. Client 2 likely has a wound infection and should be seen next, while Clients 3 and 4 have expected findings. The infected wound is tempting because fever and spreading redness are clearly abnormal, but a possible dehiscence poses the more immediate risk.
questions.takeaway: A possible dehiscence (“pop” plus a gush of pink drainage) is seen before a wound infection or expected findings.
questions.hintContent: Rank the problems by how quickly each could become life-threatening.

questions.stem: A client receiving chemotherapy for leukemia is on POD 3 after an open appendectomy. The WBC count is 1,800/mm³. The temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F); the client's baseline is 36.6 °C (97.9 °F). The incision has new tenderness and slight redness at one end. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Document expected inflammation, because the redness at the incision is only slight
Report the temperature rise and incision changes to the provider now
Recheck the temperature in 4 hours before deciding to report
Apply warm compresses to the incision to ease the tenderness
optionRationales: Incorrect. In an immunocompromised client, subtle changes may be the only sign of a serious infection.
Correct. Immunocompromised clients are at high risk for wound infection and may show only subtle signs, so new changes are reported promptly.
Incorrect. Waiting delays treatment in a client whose WBCs cannot fight infection well.
Incorrect. Warm compresses treat a symptom without addressing a possible infection and are not prescribed.
questions.rationale: Immunocompromised clients, such as those receiving chemotherapy or with leukemia, are a high-risk group for wound infection because their white blood cells cannot fight bacteria well. The same weakness blunts the usual signs, so a small temperature rise above baseline, new tenderness, and slight redness may be the only early clues. The nurse reports these changes to the provider promptly rather than waiting for dramatic findings. Documenting “expected inflammation” is tempting because the redness is mild, but in this client mild findings on POD 3 cannot be assumed to be normal.
questions.takeaway: In immunocompromised clients, subtle wound changes and small temperature rises can signal serious infection; report promptly.
questions.hintContent: Consider how a very low WBC count changes the way infection shows up.
questions.hintStrategy: When a high-risk client shows mild changes, choose prompt reporting over watchful waiting.

questions.stem: A client's evisceration has been covered with sterile saline-moistened dressings, and the client is in low Fowler's position with the knees bent while waiting for the surgical team. The client says, “My mouth is so dry. Can I have a little water?” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “A few small sips of water are fine, since you're so thirsty.”
“You can have some ice chips if you let them melt slowly.”
“Let me ask the surgeon whether you can have a few sips.”
“You need to stay NPO for surgery, but I can moisten your mouth.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Responding to thirst is caring, but even small sips break NPO status before emergency surgery and raise aspiration risk.
Incorrect. Ice chips seem like a minimal compromise, but they are still oral intake, and the client must stay NPO for surgery.
Incorrect. Checking with the surgeon seems cautious, but a client going to emergency surgery is NPO, and asking delays the comfort the nurse can give now.
Correct. The client is kept NPO in preparation for surgery; mouth care can ease dryness without oral intake.
questions.rationale: Evisceration is a surgical emergency, and the client will return to surgery. Part of the nurse's response is to keep the client NPO, which protects against aspiration under anesthesia. The nurse can still respond to the client's discomfort by moistening the lips and mouth without giving fluids to swallow. Ice chips are the tempting compromise because they seem minimal, but they are still oral intake.
questions.takeaway: A client with evisceration is NPO and prepared for surgery; offer mouth care, not fluids.
questions.hintContent: Think about what happens next for a client with evisceration and what that means for oral intake.
